Commencing prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) at 5-10 nanograms/kg/min maintains ductal patency and is life-saving in duct-dependent lesions such as transposition of the great arteries, pulmonary atresia, and critical pulmonary stenosis. The infant should be transferred to a tertiary cardiac centre. (Source: RCH CPG: Cyanotic Heart Disease; Queensland Clinical Guideline: Neonatal Stabilisation)

Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN) typically presents with labile saturations that improve then deteriorate, and often occurs in the context of meconium aspiration, sepsis, or perinatal asphyxia. A fixed cyanosis unresponsive to 100% oxygen with a failed hyperoxia test favours structural cyanotic heart disease over PPHN. (Source: RCH CPG: Cyanotic Heart Disease)

explanation.summary: Protracted bacterial bronchitis is the most common cause of chronic wet cough in preschool children. It is defined by a wet cough lasting more than 4 weeks, absence of features suggesting an alternative diagnosis, and resolution with a 14-day course of appropriate antibiotics. The TSANZ cough guideline recommends amoxicillin-clavulanate as first-line therapy. If the cough recurs more than three times in 12 months, investigation for underlying conditions such as primary ciliary dyskinesia, immunodeficiency, or bronchiectasis is warranted. Untreated PBB may progress to bronchiectasis.
key_points: PBB is defined as wet cough for more than 4 weeks without alternative diagnosis, resolving with antibiotics
Amoxicillin-clavulanate for 14 days is first-line therapy per TSANZ guidelines
Common pathogens are non-typeable Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Moraxella catarrhalis
Recurrent PBB (more than 3 episodes per year) warrants investigation for bronchiectasis, immunodeficiency, or PCD
The key distinguishing feature from asthma is a wet (not dry) cough with no wheeze and no bronchodilator response
explanation.pearls: Untreated protracted bacterial bronchitis may progress to bronchiectasis via the 'vicious cycle' hypothesis - chronic bacterial infection leads to neutrophilic airway inflammation, impaired mucociliary clearance, and progressive airway damage within 1-2 years of recurrent episodes.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic Cough in Children

options.rationale: Asthma typically presents with episodic wheeze, dry cough worse at night or with exercise, and response to bronchodilators. This child has a persistent wet cough with no wheeze, no nocturnal symptoms, no exercise limitation, and no bronchodilator response, making asthma unlikely. An ICS trial is not appropriate without asthma features. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic Cough in Children)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic Cough in Children

options.rationale: Cystic fibrosis should be considered in children with recurrent wet cough, but this child is thriving with a normal CXR and this is his first prolonged episode. Sweat chloride testing becomes appropriate if the cough recurs after adequate antibiotic treatment or if there are other red flags such as failure to thrive, steatorrhoea, or recurrent pneumonia. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic Cough in Children)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic Cough in Children

options.rationale: This presentation is classic for protracted bacterial bronchitis (PBB): a wet productive cough for more than 4 weeks in an otherwise well child with no features of an alternative diagnosis and a normal CXR. First-line treatment per TSANZ guidelines is a 14-day course of amoxicillin-clavulanate, targeting the common pathogens (Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Moraxella catarrhalis). Resolution of cough with antibiotics confirms the diagnosis. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic Cough in Children; eTG: Respiratory)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic Cough in Children

options.rationale: CT chest is not indicated as a first-line investigation for chronic wet cough in a well child with a normal CXR. It is reserved for children who fail to respond to appropriate antibiotic therapy or who have red flag features suggesting bronchiectasis or structural abnormality. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic Cough in Children)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic Cough in Children

options.rationale: Post-viral cough is typically dry and resolves within 3-4 weeks. A wet productive cough persisting beyond 4 weeks is not consistent with post-viral aetiology and warrants investigation and treatment. Observation alone risks progression to bronchiectasis. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic Cough in Children)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic Cough in Children

explanation.summary: Vesicoureteral reflux management depends on grade, presence of renal scarring, and frequency of breakthrough UTIs. Low-grade VUR (I-III) without scarring often resolves spontaneously and may be managed conservatively. High-grade VUR (IV-V) with renal scarring carries a higher risk of progressive renal damage and warrants continuous antibiotic prophylaxis. Surgical intervention (open reimplantation or endoscopic injection) is reserved for cases failing medical management. Serial imaging monitors for reflux resolution and new scarring.
key_points: VUR is graded I-V based on the degree of ureteric dilatation and calyceal blunting on MCUG
Antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended for high-grade VUR with renal scarring to prevent further damage
Spontaneous resolution rates decrease with increasing VUR grade: approximately 80% for grade I-II vs 30% for grade IV
DMSA scan is the gold standard for detecting renal cortical scarring
Surgical reimplantation is reserved for breakthrough febrile UTIs on prophylaxis or non-resolving high-grade reflux
explanation.pearls: Trimethoprim at one-third of the therapeutic dose given as a single nightly dose is the standard prophylactic regimen for VUR in Australian practice - nitrofurantoin is an alternative but is avoided in infants under 1 month due to haemolytic risk.

options.rationale: Observation alone may be appropriate for low-grade VUR (grades I-II) without renal scarring. This child has grade IV reflux with documented renal scarring and recurrent febrile UTIs, warranting a more proactive approach to prevent further renal damage. (Source: RCH CPG: Vesicoureteral Reflux; KHA-CARI Guidelines)

Treating only acute episodes without prophylaxis exposes the scarred kidney to further damage with each febrile UTI. In a child with high-grade reflux and existing renal scarring, the risk of progressive renal damage from recurrent pyelonephritis is significant. (Source: KHA-CARI Guidelines)

Surgical reimplantation is effective for high-grade VUR but is not the immediate first step. A trial of antibiotic prophylaxis is generally recommended first, with surgery reserved for breakthrough febrile UTIs on prophylaxis, worsening renal scarring, or non-resolution of high-grade reflux. The grade II right side is also unlikely to require surgery. (Source: RCH CPG: Vesicoureteral Reflux)

Endoscopic injection (e.g. Deflux) is an option for VUR but has lower success rates for grade IV-V reflux compared with open reimplantation. It is not the recommended first-line approach before trialling antibiotic prophylaxis, especially for high-grade reflux with renal scarring. (Source: RCH CPG: Vesicoureteral Reflux)

For a young child with recurrent febrile UTIs, grade IV VUR, and existing renal scarring, continuous antibiotic prophylaxis (e.g. trimethoprim) is recommended to reduce UTI recurrence while allowing time for spontaneous resolution. Regular follow-up includes repeat MCUG at 12-18 months and repeat DMSA if breakthrough UTIs occur. If breakthrough febrile UTIs occur on prophylaxis, surgical options should be discussed. (Source: RCH CPG: Vesicoureteral Reflux; KHA-CARI Guidelines)

explanation.summary: JIA-associated anterior uveitis is the most common extra-articular complication of oligoarticular JIA. It is characteristically chronic, bilateral, and asymptomatic (white eye) - children do not complain of pain or redness. Risk factors for uveitis include young age at JIA onset (under 7 years), ANA positivity, oligoarticular subtype, and female sex. Without regular slit-lamp screening, up to 30% of high-risk children develop uveitis-related complications including posterior synechiae, cataracts, and glaucoma. Screening frequency is determined by risk stratification.
key_points: JIA-associated uveitis is chronic and asymptomatic - slit-lamp examination is the only way to detect it early
Highest risk: ANA-positive, oligoarticular JIA, onset under 7 years, female
Screening frequency for high-risk patients is every 3 months for the first 4 years after JIA diagnosis
Complications of undetected uveitis include posterior synechiae, band keratopathy, cataracts, glaucoma, and blindness
Uveitis can precede, coincide with, or follow the onset of arthritis
explanation.pearls: JIA-associated uveitis is a 'white eye' uveitis - the absence of conjunctival redness, pain, or photophobia means it is invisible to parents and GPs, and slit-lamp screening is the only reliable detection method for the first 7 years after JIA diagnosis.

options.rationale: This child has the highest-risk profile for JIA-associated uveitis: young age at onset (under 7 years), oligoarticular JIA, and ANA-positive. JIA-associated anterior uveitis is typically chronic and asymptomatic (no pain or redness), meaning it can only be detected by slit-lamp examination. Without screening, uveitis can progress to posterior synechiae, cataract, band keratopathy, and blindness. Australian and international guidelines recommend 3-monthly slit-lamp review for high-risk patients. (Source: RACS/RACP Guidelines: JIA Uveitis Screening; Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

Cardiac involvement is a feature of acute rheumatic fever, not JIA. JIA does not cause valvular disease. Pericarditis can occur in systemic-onset JIA but not oligoarticular JIA, and routine echocardiography is not indicated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

Renal involvement is not a feature of JIA. Nephritis is associated with systemic lupus erythematosus, IgA vasculitis, and other conditions but not with oligoarticular JIA. ANA positivity in JIA predicts uveitis risk, not renal disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

Osteoporosis screening may be considered in children on prolonged systemic corticosteroids or with systemic JIA, but is not routine for newly diagnosed oligoarticular JIA. This child's disease can likely be managed with intra-articular corticosteroids and does not require systemic therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

LFT monitoring is required for children on methotrexate, but this child has just been diagnosed and methotrexate has not been started. Oligoarticular JIA is often managed with intra-articular corticosteroid injections as first-line, with methotrexate reserved for refractory or polyarticular disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

explanation.summary: Langerhans cell histiocytosis is a clonal proliferation of pathological Langerhans-type dendritic cells that can affect virtually any organ. The classic triad of skull lytic lesions, diabetes insipidus, and exophthalmos (Hand-Schuller-Christian disease) is rare, but multisystem LCH in young children commonly involves skin, bone, liver, and the pituitary stalk. The seborrhoeic dermatitis-like rash of LCH is often misdiagnosed as cradle cap or fungal infection. Diabetes insipidus from pituitary stalk infiltration occurs in 15-25% of multisystem cases. Diagnosis requires tissue biopsy demonstrating CD1a-positive and CD207-positive histiocytes.
key_points: LCH skin involvement mimics seborrhoeic dermatitis but fails to respond to standard treatment
Well-defined 'punched-out' lytic bone lesions without sclerotic margins are characteristic on plain X-ray
Diabetes insipidus indicates pituitary stalk infiltration and occurs in 15-25% of multisystem LCH
Diagnosis requires CD1a and CD207 (langerin) positivity on immunohistochemistry of biopsied tissue
Risk organ involvement (liver, spleen, bone marrow) determines prognosis and treatment intensity
explanation.pearls: In children under 2 years, LCH involving risk organs (liver, spleen, or bone marrow) carries a mortality of 10-20% despite chemotherapy - early identification of hepatomegaly and cytopenias is critical for risk stratification.

options.rationale: The rash has already failed antifungal therapy and the combination of a seborrhoea-like rash with a lytic skull lesion, hepatomegaly, and diabetes insipidus is strongly suggestive of a systemic infiltrative process rather than a dermatophyte infection. (Source: RCH CPG: Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis)

The combination of a seborrhoea-like rash refractory to antifungals, a punched-out lytic skull lesion, hepatomegaly, anaemia, and diabetes insipidus (polyuria with dilute urine and hypernatraemia) is the classic multisystem presentation of Langerhans cell histiocytosis. Tissue biopsy with positive CD1a and CD207 (langerin) immunohistochemistry on the infiltrating cells confirms the diagnosis. Birbeck granules on electron microscopy are the historical gold standard. (Source: RCH CPG: Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis; Histiocyte Society Guidelines)

Neuroblastoma can cause lytic bone lesions but typically presents with a primary abdominal or thoracic mass, proptosis from orbital metastases, or raccoon eyes. The combination of seborrhoeic rash, punched-out lytic lesion, and diabetes insipidus is more characteristic of LCH. MIBG scan is the staging investigation for neuroblastoma. (Source: RCH CPG: Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis)

Acute leukaemia can cause bone pain, hepatomegaly, and cytopenias, but does not typically cause well-defined lytic skull lesions or a seborrhoeic rash. While bone marrow assessment may be part of the LCH staging workup, the diagnostic biopsy should target the most accessible lesion - in this case the skull or skin. (Source: Histiocyte Society Guidelines)

The clinical picture of polyuria with dilute urine (specific gravity 1.002) and hypernatraemia is consistent with diabetes insipidus, but confirming DI alone does not identify the underlying cause. The priority is to diagnose the systemic disease causing the DI - tissue biopsy is the key investigation. (Source: RCH CPG: Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis)

explanation.summary: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura) nephritis occurs in up to 50% of affected children, usually within the first 3 months. Most have mild disease with isolated haematuria that resolves spontaneously. However, significant proteinuria (uPCR > 100 mg/mmol), nephrotic syndrome, hypertension, or impaired renal function indicate moderate-to-severe nephritis requiring renal biopsy. The ISKDC classification grades severity from I (minimal change) to VI (membranoproliferative) and guides immunosuppressive therapy. Long-term renal outcomes are excellent for mild disease but 5-10% of those with nephritis develop chronic kidney disease.
key_points: Nephritis occurs in up to 50% of IgA vasculitis cases, usually within the first 3 months
Renal biopsy is indicated for nephrotic-range proteinuria (uPCR > 100 mg/mmol), nephrotic syndrome, or impaired renal function
Urinalysis should be monitored weekly for 4 weeks then monthly for 6 months after IgA vasculitis diagnosis
ISKDC classification on biopsy guides treatment - grades III-V may require immunosuppression
Normal complement levels help distinguish IgA vasculitis nephritis from post-infectious glomerulonephritis and lupus nephritis
explanation.pearls: Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio above 100 mg/mmol in IgA vasculitis nephritis is the commonly used threshold for renal biopsy - this corresponds to approximately 1 g/day proteinuria and predicts ISKDC grade III or higher on histology.

options.rationale: While mild microscopic haematuria alone may be observed in IgA vasculitis, this child has significant proteinuria (uPCR 120 mg/mmol), hypertension, and hypoalbuminaemia - indicating nephritis with nephrotic-range features. This requires active management rather than simple observation. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein Purpura; KDIGO Glomerulonephritis Guidelines)

ACE inhibitors are appropriate for reducing proteinuria and controlling hypertension, and may be started. However, the degree of proteinuria and hypoalbuminaemia in this child suggests significant glomerular involvement that may require biopsy before deciding on immunosuppressive therapy. Starting prednisolone without histological confirmation of the severity risks under-treating or over-treating. (Source: KDIGO Glomerulonephritis Guidelines)

Serum IgA may be elevated in IgA vasculitis but is not specific and does not change management. ANCA testing is relevant for ANCA-associated vasculitis (GPA, MPA) but IgA vasculitis is not ANCA-associated. The diagnosis is clinical and additional serological testing does not inform the management of nephritis. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein Purpura)

This child has IgA vasculitis nephritis with nephrotic-range proteinuria (uPCR > 100 mg/mmol), hypertension, and hypoalbuminaemia. These features indicate moderate-to-severe glomerular involvement and meet the threshold for renal biopsy. Biopsy determines the ISKDC histological grade (I-VI), which guides immunosuppressive therapy. Nephrology referral is essential for biopsy and ongoing management. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein Purpura; KDIGO Glomerulonephritis Guidelines)

IV methylprednisolone may be used for severe crescentic IgA vasculitis nephritis, but should not be commenced without first obtaining a renal biopsy to confirm the severity and guide treatment. Starting aggressive immunosuppression empirically risks unnecessary toxicity if the histological grade does not warrant it. (Source: KDIGO Glomerulonephritis Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Acute pancreatitis in children is increasingly recognised, with drug-induced causes (valproate, azathioprine, L-asparaginase) being an important aetiology alongside biliary, traumatic, and idiopathic causes. Modern management has shifted away from prolonged bowel rest toward early enteral feeding within 24-48 hours. Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation reduces the risk of pancreatic necrosis. Valproate-induced pancreatitis typically occurs within the first year of treatment and requires drug cessation and alternative anticonvulsant selection. Severity is assessed by clinical parameters and imaging.
key_points: Serum lipase is more sensitive and specific than amylase for diagnosing acute pancreatitis
Early enteral nutrition within 24-48 hours is superior to prolonged bowel rest and TPN
Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation (1.5-2 times maintenance) reduces the risk of necrosis
Valproate is a recognised cause of pancreatitis in children and should be discontinued
Prophylactic antibiotics are not indicated in acute pancreatitis
explanation.pearls: Valproate-induced pancreatitis can occur at any time during treatment but most cases present within the first year - the drug must be permanently discontinued and never re-challenged, as recurrence risk exceeds 50% on re-exposure.

options.rationale: ERCP is indicated for biliary pancreatitis with choledocholithiasis and cholangitis. This child has no gallstones on ultrasound, no bile duct dilatation, and normal bilirubin and ALT, making biliary obstruction unlikely. The likely aetiology is drug-induced (valproate). (Source: NASPGHAN: Paediatric Pancreatitis)

Prolonged bowel rest and TPN are no longer recommended for acute pancreatitis. Early enteral feeding (within 24-48 hours) is associated with shorter hospital stays, fewer complications, and reduced infectious morbidity. TPN is reserved for patients who cannot tolerate enteral feeding after 5-7 days. (Source: NASPGHAN: Paediatric Pancreatitis; eTG: Gastrointestinal)

Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended for acute pancreatitis as they do not reduce the risk of infected necrosis and promote antimicrobial resistance. Antibiotics are only indicated if there is documented infected necrosis or concurrent cholangitis. (Source: NASPGHAN: Paediatric Pancreatitis)

The management of acute pancreatitis in children centres on aggressive IV fluid resuscitation (1.5-2 times maintenance crystalloid), effective analgesia (paracetamol, opioids if needed), and early enteral nutrition within 24-48 hours as tolerated. Valproate should be reviewed as a likely causative agent. Monitoring for complications (necrosis, pseudocyst, organ failure) with serial lipase and clinical assessment is essential. (Source: NASPGHAN: Paediatric Pancreatitis; RCH CPG: Pancreatitis)

Surgical necrosectomy is reserved for infected pancreatic necrosis confirmed by fine-needle aspiration or clinical deterioration, and is typically delayed until at least 4 weeks to allow walled-off necrosis to mature. Imaging shows peripancreatic fluid but not established necrosis, and surgery at this stage is premature. (Source: NASPGHAN: Paediatric Pancreatitis)

explanation.summary: Paediatric obstructive sleep apnoea affects 1-5% of children and is most commonly caused by adenotonsillar hypertrophy in the 2-8 year age group. Polysomnography is the gold standard for diagnosis and severity assessment. An oAHI greater than 1 event per hour is abnormal in children. Adenotonsillectomy is first-line treatment for moderate-to-severe OSA with adenotonsillar hypertrophy, with cure rates of 70-80%. Children with severe OSA require post-operative monitoring due to increased risk of respiratory complications. Persistent OSA after surgery warrants CPAP therapy.
key_points: Adenotonsillectomy is first-line treatment for paediatric OSA caused by adenotonsillar hypertrophy
An obstructive AHI greater than 1 per hour is abnormal in children (unlike adults where the threshold is 5)
Post-operative monitoring is recommended for oAHI greater than 10, SpO2 nadir below 85%, or age under 3 years
Intranasal corticosteroids may be trialled for mild OSA (oAHI 1-5) but are insufficient for moderate-to-severe disease
Residual OSA after adenotonsillectomy occurs in 20-30% of cases and may require CPAP
explanation.pearls: The paediatric oAHI threshold for abnormality is 1 event per hour - far lower than the adult threshold of 5 - reflecting the developing brain's greater vulnerability to intermittent hypoxia and sleep fragmentation.

options.rationale: Intranasal corticosteroids may be trialled for mild OSA (oAHI 1-5) or as an adjunct, but this child has moderate-to-severe OSA with an oAHI of 12 and significant desaturations. Medical therapy alone is inadequate for this severity. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Paediatric OSA; RCH CPG: Obstructive Sleep Apnoea)

CPAP is second-line for paediatric OSA and is reserved for children who are not surgical candidates, who have persistent OSA after adenotonsillectomy, or who have conditions where surgery is unlikely to be curative (e.g. obesity, craniofacial abnormalities). In a child with adenotonsillar hypertrophy as the primary cause, surgery is first-line. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Paediatric OSA)

This child's BMI is at the 75th centile, which is normal weight. While obesity worsens OSA, it is not the primary driver here - the grade 3+ tonsillar hypertrophy is the clear anatomical cause. Delaying treatment for a year risks neurocognitive and cardiovascular consequences of untreated moderate-to-severe OSA. (Source: RCH CPG: Obstructive Sleep Apnoea)

Mandibular advancement devices are used in adult OSA but are not recommended in children due to the growing craniofacial skeleton. Adenotonsillectomy is the first-line surgical treatment for paediatric OSA caused by lymphoid hypertrophy. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Paediatric OSA)

Adenotonsillectomy is the first-line treatment for moderate-to-severe paediatric OSA due to adenotonsillar hypertrophy. This child has an oAHI of 12 (moderate-severe), significant desaturations, and grade 3+ tonsils. The CHAT trial demonstrated significant improvements in behaviour, quality of life, and polysomnographic parameters after surgery. Post-operative monitoring in hospital is recommended given the severity of his OSA due to increased risk of post-operative respiratory complications. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Paediatric OSA; RCH CPG: Obstructive Sleep Apnoea)

explanation.summary: Laryngomalacia is the most common cause of stridor in infants, accounting for 60-70% of congenital stridor. It is caused by collapse of the supraglottic structures during inspiration due to immature cartilaginous support. Symptoms typically onset in the first 2-4 weeks of life, peak at 6-8 months, and resolve by 12-24 months. Most cases are mild and self-limiting. Severe laryngomalacia (failure to thrive, cyanotic episodes, obstructive sleep apnoea) occurs in 10-15% of cases and may require supraglottoplasty. Flexible nasendoscopy is the diagnostic investigation of choice.
key_points: Laryngomalacia accounts for 60-70% of congenital stridor in infants
Classic features: inspiratory stridor worsening in supine position and during feeding, improving when prone
Flexible nasendoscopy performed awake is the gold standard diagnostic investigation
Most cases are mild and self-limiting, resolving by 12-24 months
Supraglottoplasty is indicated for severe cases with failure to thrive, cyanosis, or cor pulmonale
explanation.pearls: Approximately 15-20% of infants with laryngomalacia have a synchronous second airway lesion (subglottic stenosis, tracheomalacia, or vocal cord palsy) - if symptoms are disproportionately severe for the degree of laryngomalacia seen on flexible scope, a full airway assessment under general anaesthesia is warranted.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Flexible nasendoscopy (fibre-optic laryngoscopy) performed awake in clinic is the gold standard for diagnosing laryngomalacia. It directly visualises the supraglottic structures and demonstrates the characteristic omega-shaped epiglottis with prolapse of the aryepiglottic folds during inspiration. It can be performed at the bedside without sedation and also excludes other causes of stridor such as vocal cord palsy or subglottic lesions. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor in Children; Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: A lateral neck X-ray may show the 'steeple sign' in croup or a retropharyngeal mass, but has poor sensitivity for laryngomalacia. The supraglottic structures are not well visualised on plain film. Direct visualisation with flexible endoscopy is far superior. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor in Children)

CT neck exposes the infant to ionising radiation and requires sedation, which can worsen airway obstruction. It is reserved for suspected vascular rings, deep neck infections, or complex airway abnormalities not diagnosable by endoscopy. Laryngomalacia is best diagnosed by direct visualisation. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor in Children)

Rigid microlaryngoscopy and bronchoscopy (MLB) under general anaesthesia provides the most comprehensive airway assessment but is reserved for severe cases requiring intervention (supraglottoplasty), diagnostic uncertainty after flexible endoscopy, or suspected synchronous airway lesions. An awake flexible scope is the appropriate first investigation. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor in Children)

A barium swallow can identify extrinsic oesophageal compression from a vascular ring, which typically causes biphasic (inspiratory and expiratory) stridor and feeding difficulties. This infant has purely inspiratory stridor that worsens in the supine position - a pattern more consistent with supraglottic collapse (laryngomalacia) than vascular compression. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor in Children)

explanation.summary: Childhood obesity above the 95th centile BMI warrants metabolic screening for comorbidities. The NHMRC guidelines recommend fasting lipids, fasting glucose, HbA1c, and liver function tests as the core metabolic panel. Acanthosis nigricans is a cutaneous marker of insulin resistance and should prompt glucose metabolism assessment. Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease affects up to 40% of obese children and is detected by elevated ALT. Lifestyle modification (healthy eating, physical activity, reduced screen time) is the cornerstone of management, with pharmacotherapy (metformin, liraglutide) reserved for specific circumstances.
key_points: BMI above the 95th centile in children warrants metabolic screening with fasting lipids, glucose, HbA1c, and LFTs
Acanthosis nigricans indicates insulin resistance and increases the risk of type 2 diabetes
Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (ALT elevation) affects up to 40% of obese children
Normal height velocity makes endocrine causes of obesity (hypothyroidism, Cushing) very unlikely
Family history of type 2 diabetes is a major risk factor for childhood insulin resistance
explanation.pearls: In an obese child, a normal or tall height centile with crossing weight centiles indicates exogenous (multifactorial) obesity - a short or falling height centile with rising weight should prompt investigation for endocrine causes including Cushing syndrome and hypothyroidism.

sources.label: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guidelines for Obesity

options.rationale: While an OGTT can diagnose impaired glucose tolerance and type 2 diabetes, fasting glucose and HbA1c are the recommended initial screening tests in Australian guidelines for paediatric obesity. An OGTT is reserved for equivocal results or high-risk populations. Fasting insulin is not routinely recommended as there is no standardised paediatric reference range. (Source: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guidelines for Obesity; RCH CPG: Obesity)
source_refs: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guidelines for Obesity

options.rationale: Australian guidelines recommend a comprehensive metabolic screen for children with obesity (BMI above the 95th centile) including fasting lipid profile (total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides), fasting glucose, HbA1c, and liver function tests (screening for non-alcoholic fatty liver disease). Acanthosis nigricans and a family history of type 2 diabetes increase the risk of insulin resistance and dyslipidaemia. (Source: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guidelines for Obesity; RCH CPG: Obesity; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guidelines for Obesity

options.rationale: Hypothyroidism and Cushing syndrome are rare causes of obesity in children. Thyroid function may be checked but is not the most appropriate initial screen on its own. Hypothyroidism causing obesity is almost always associated with short stature - this child is at the 75th centile for height, making endocrine causes unlikely. (Source: RCH CPG: Obesity)

Monogenic obesity (leptin deficiency, MC4R mutations) is extremely rare and typically presents with severe early-onset obesity before age 2 years, extreme hyperphagia, and sometimes associated features. This 10-year-old's presentation is consistent with common multifactorial obesity. Genetic testing is not indicated as an initial screen. (Source: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guidelines for Obesity)
source_refs: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guidelines for Obesity

options.rationale: Polysomnography is indicated if there are symptoms of obstructive sleep apnoea, but this child has no OSA symptoms. Echocardiography is not part of routine metabolic screening for childhood obesity unless there are cardiac symptoms or signs. These investigations may be considered but are not the appropriate initial metabolic screen. (Source: RCH CPG: Obesity)

explanation.summary: Congenital syphilis rates have risen sharply in Australia, particularly in northern and central Australia. Adequate maternal treatment requires benzathine penicillin administered at least 30 days before delivery with a documented four-fold decline in RPR titre. When these criteria are not met, the neonate must be treated presumptively with 10 days of IV benzylpenicillin regardless of clinical appearance, as early congenital syphilis may be asymptomatic at birth. The workup includes FBC, LFTs, long bone X-rays, ophthalmology review, audiology, and lumbar puncture.
key_points: Adequate maternal syphilis treatment requires benzathine penicillin at least 30 days before delivery with documented serological response
IV benzylpenicillin for 10 days is the standard treatment for presumed congenital syphilis
Up to 60% of neonates with congenital syphilis are asymptomatic at birth - normal examination does not exclude infection
Follow-up serology at 3, 6, and 12 months is required to confirm treatment response
Congenital syphilis rates have increased significantly in Australia since 2015, particularly in remote Aboriginal communities
explanation.pearls: A neonatal RPR titre equal to or less than the maternal titre may represent passive transfer of antibodies, but a titre four-fold or greater above the maternal titre is diagnostic of congenital infection - however, treatment should never be delayed for titre comparison when maternal treatment is inadequate.

options.rationale: Maternal treatment with a single dose of benzathine penicillin at 33 weeks is inadequate. Adequate treatment requires benzathine penicillin administered at least 30 days before delivery, with documented serological response (four-fold RPR titre decline). A single dose given 7 weeks before delivery without follow-up serology does not meet criteria for adequate treatment. (Source: ASHM: Australian STI Management Guidelines; SA Health: Congenital Syphilis)

While serial serology is required for monitoring, delaying treatment to observe titre trends is inappropriate when maternal treatment is inadequate. Passively transferred maternal antibodies may decline regardless of neonatal infection status, and untreated congenital syphilis can cause irreversible damage. (Source: ASHM: Australian STI Management Guidelines)

When maternal treatment is inadequate (administered less than 30 days before delivery, incomplete course, or no documented serological response), the neonate should be treated presumptively for congenital syphilis regardless of clinical appearance. The standard regimen is IV benzylpenicillin (50 mg/kg/dose, 12-hourly in the first week then 8-hourly for the remaining days) for 10 days. Follow-up serology at 3, 6, and 12 months confirms treatment response. (Source: ASHM: Australian STI Management Guidelines; SA Health: Congenital Syphilis)

A single dose of IM benzathine penicillin may be appropriate only if the neonate is fully investigated and all results are normal AND the mother was adequately treated. When maternal treatment is inadequate, a single dose is insufficient and the full 10-day IV regimen is required. (Source: ASHM: Australian STI Management Guidelines)

Lumbar puncture to assess for neurosyphilis (CSF VDRL, cell count, protein) is part of the workup for congenital syphilis and should be performed before starting treatment. However, treatment should not be withheld pending CSF results, and a normal CSF does not change the need for a 10-day IV course when maternal treatment is inadequate. (Source: SA Health: Congenital Syphilis)

explanation.summary: Congenital long QT syndrome presenting as 2:1 AV block in a neonate is a rare but life-threatening presentation. The mechanism is functional rather than structural: the QT interval is so prolonged that every other atrial impulse arrives during the ventricular refractory period, creating pseudo-2:1 block. T-wave alternans on the neonatal ECG is a hallmark sign and indicates high arrhythmic risk. This presentation carries greater than 50% mortality in the first year without treatment. Genetic testing identifies the channel mutation (KCNQ1 in LQT1, KCNH2 in LQT2, SCN5A in LQT3), which guides genotype-specific management.
key_points: 2:1 AV block with markedly prolonged QTc in a neonate is functional LQTS, not structural heart block
T-wave alternans is a hallmark ECG sign indicating high torsades de pointes risk
IV magnesium sulfate is the immediate stabilisation measure, followed by beta-blocker initiation
Mortality exceeds 50% in the first year without treatment for neonatal LQTS presenting as 2:1 block
Genetic testing for KCNQ1 (LQT1), KCNH2 (LQT2), and SCN5A (LQT3) guides genotype-specific therapy
explanation.pearls: Neonatal 2:1 AV block with a QTc above 600 ms is almost always functional LQTS, not structural conduction disease - the QT interval is so long that every second P wave falls in the ventricular refractory period, and beta-blockade (not pacing alone) is the life-saving treatment.

options.rationale: Autoimmune congenital heart block from maternal anti-Ro/anti-La antibodies causes isolated complete heart block but does not prolong the QTc interval. Maternal antibodies are negative in this case. The combination of 2:1 AV block, markedly prolonged QTc (620 ms), and T-wave alternans is diagnostic of congenital long QT syndrome, not autoimmune heart block. (Source: RCH CPG: Cardiac Arrhythmias; CSANZ: Inherited Cardiac Conditions)

Neonatal myocarditis typically presents with heart failure, poor feeding, and ventricular dysfunction on echocardiography. This neonate has a structurally and functionally normal heart. The markedly prolonged QTc with 2:1 AV block and T-wave alternans is characteristic of channelopathy, not myocarditis. (Source: RCH CPG: Cardiac Arrhythmias)

Hypocalcaemia and hypomagnesaemia can prolong the QTc interval but do not typically cause 2:1 AV block or T-wave alternans. A QTc of 620 ms in a well-appearing neonate with normal feeding is far more consistent with a congenital channelopathy than a transient electrolyte disturbance. Electrolytes should be checked and corrected if abnormal, but this is not the primary diagnosis. (Source: CSANZ: Inherited Cardiac Conditions)

The combination of 2:1 AV block with markedly prolonged QTc (620 ms) and T-wave alternans in a neonate with a structurally normal heart and negative maternal autoantibodies is diagnostic of congenital long QT syndrome presenting with functional 2:1 AV block (the QT interval is so long that every other P wave falls during the refractory period). This is a high-risk presentation with mortality exceeding 50% in the first year without treatment. Immediate management includes IV magnesium sulfate to stabilise the myocardium, followed by initiation of a beta-blocker (propranolol or nadolol). Temporary pacing may be needed. Genetic testing for KCNQ1, KCNH2, and SCN5A mutations guides long-term management. (Source: CSANZ: Inherited Cardiac Conditions; Heart Rhythm Society: LQTS Guidelines)

While this neonate has a ventricular rate of 48 bpm which typically warrants consideration of pacing, the underlying diagnosis is critical. The markedly prolonged QTc and T-wave alternans indicate that the 2:1 AV block is functional (related to the extremely long repolarisation period in LQTS) rather than structural conduction disease. Pacing without addressing the underlying channelopathy (with magnesium and beta-blockade) risks triggering torsades de pointes. (Source: CSANZ: Inherited Cardiac Conditions)

explanation.summary: Macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) is a life-threatening complication of systemic JIA, occurring in 10-15% of sJIA patients. It is characterised by uncontrolled macrophage and T-cell activation with a cytokine storm. The key diagnostic clues are paradoxical changes: falling ESR (from fibrinogen consumption), falling WCC and platelets (from previously elevated levels in sJIA), and massively rising ferritin. MAS shares criteria with secondary haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH). Treatment is high-dose corticosteroids with ciclosporin as second-line. Mortality without treatment approaches 20-30%.
key_points: Paradoxically falling ESR in active sJIA is a red flag for MAS (ESR falls because fibrinogen is consumed)
Ferritin above 10,000 microg/L in sJIA is highly suggestive of MAS
Falling WCC and platelets FROM previously elevated levels (not just low counts) is characteristic
First-line: IV methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg (max 1 g) daily for 3 days; second-line: ciclosporin A
Anakinra dose escalation (up to 10 mg/kg/day) is increasingly used as adjunctive therapy in sJIA-MAS
explanation.pearls: The most specific early warning sign of MAS in sJIA is a paradoxical fall in ESR while ferritin rises - this discordance occurs because fibrinogen (the main determinant of ESR) is consumed by DIC while ferritin is released by activated macrophages.

options.rationale: While IL-1 blockade (anakinra) is used in sJIA-MAS, increasing the dose alone is insufficient for established MAS with organ dysfunction. This child has life-threatening MAS with encephalopathy, coagulopathy, and cytopenias. High-dose corticosteroids are the first-line treatment for MAS. Anakinra dose escalation may be appropriate as adjunctive therapy but not as the primary intervention. (Source: PRINTO/PRES: MAS Classification Criteria; Ravelli et al, Ann Rheum Dis 2016)

While sepsis can mimic or trigger MAS and blood cultures should be drawn, the clinical picture (paradoxically falling ESR, soaring ferritin, falling fibrinogen, falling counts from previously elevated levels, hepatosplenomegaly in a child with sJIA) is characteristic of MAS. Treatment must target the immune dysregulation, not just infection. Antibiotics alone will not address the cytokine storm. (Source: PRINTO/PRES: MAS Classification Criteria)

This child has fulminant macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) complicating sJIA, evidenced by the paradoxical fall in ESR and WCC (from previously high levels), massively elevated ferritin (above 10,000 microg/L), falling fibrinogen (DIC), encephalopathy, cytopenias, and organ dysfunction. First-line treatment is high-dose IV methylprednisolone (30 mg/kg, max 1 g, daily for 3 days) followed by oral dexamethasone. Ciclosporin A is added as second-line or concurrently in severe cases. ICU admission is essential for haemodynamic monitoring and management of coagulopathy. Anakinra dose escalation may be added. (Source: PRINTO/PRES: MAS Classification Criteria; ACR/EULAR sJIA-MAS Treatment Recommendations)

Blood product support (FFP, cryoprecipitate for fibrinogen, platelets) is important supportive care for the consumptive coagulopathy, but does not address the underlying immune dysregulation driving MAS. Without immunosuppressive treatment, the cytokine storm will continue consuming blood products. Observation without immunosuppression risks rapid deterioration and death. (Source: PRINTO/PRES: MAS Classification Criteria)

The HLH-2004 protocol (etoposide, dexamethasone, ciclosporin) is used for primary (genetic) haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. MAS complicating sJIA is a secondary form that typically responds to corticosteroids and ciclosporin without the need for etoposide. Etoposide is reserved for refractory MAS not responding to first-line immunosuppression. (Source: ACR/EULAR sJIA-MAS Treatment Recommendations)

explanation.summary: Leigh syndrome (subacute necrotising encephalomyelopathy) is the most common paediatric mitochondrial disorder, caused by defects in mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. It presents with developmental regression, movement disorders, and brainstem dysfunction in infancy or early childhood. The hallmark is bilateral symmetric basal ganglia and brainstem lesions on MRI. The elevated lactate-to-pyruvate ratio above 20 indicates impaired oxidative phosphorylation. Maternal inheritance (through a maternal uncle) suggests a mitochondrial DNA mutation. Over 75 nuclear and mitochondrial genes have been implicated. There is no curative treatment; management is supportive with cofactor supplementation.
key_points: Leigh syndrome shows bilateral symmetric T2-hyperintense lesions in the basal ganglia and brainstem on MRI
Elevated lactate-to-pyruvate ratio above 20 indicates impaired mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation
CSF lactate is often elevated even when blood lactate is normal, reflecting CNS metabolic dysfunction
Maternal inheritance pattern suggests mitochondrial DNA mutation (maternally inherited through mothers to all children)
Episodic metabolic decompensation during intercurrent illness is characteristic of mitochondrial disease
explanation.pearls: In Leigh syndrome, the lactate-to-pyruvate ratio above 20 distinguishes mitochondrial respiratory chain defects (elevated ratio) from pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency (normal or low ratio) - both cause lactic acidosis and basal ganglia lesions, but the treatment implications differ (ketogenic diet for PDH deficiency, cofactor supplementation for respiratory chain defects).

options.rationale: Genetic testing is the ultimate confirmatory investigation for mitochondrial disease but requires targeted analysis informed by the clinical and imaging phenotype. While whole exome sequencing will eventually be performed, MRI brain should be obtained first as the characteristic Leigh syndrome pattern (bilateral symmetric basal ganglia and brainstem lesions) narrows the differential and guides genetic testing priorities. (Source: RCPCH: Mitochondrial Disease; GeneReviews: Leigh Syndrome)

Muscle biopsy with mitochondrial respiratory chain enzyme analysis was historically the gold standard for diagnosing mitochondrial disorders. However, it is invasive, may show normal results in some mitochondrial diseases (especially mtDNA mutations with tissue mosaicism), and has been largely superseded by genetic testing as the primary diagnostic tool. It remains useful when genetic testing is inconclusive. (Source: RCPCH: Mitochondrial Disease)

Fibroblast culture is less invasive than muscle biopsy but requires 4-6 weeks for cell growth and has lower sensitivity than muscle tissue. It is not the first-line investigation for a child with a classic clinical presentation and biochemical profile. Imaging should precede invasive tissue testing. (Source: GeneReviews: Leigh Syndrome)

While seizures occur in mitochondrial disease, EEG is not the diagnostic investigation. This child's presentation is one of developmental regression with movement disorder and metabolic derangement, not primarily epilepsy. EEG may be useful for seizure characterisation but does not confirm the underlying mitochondrial diagnosis. (Source: RCPCH: Mitochondrial Disease)

MRI brain is the most appropriate next investigation. Leigh syndrome characteristically shows bilateral symmetric T2-hyperintense lesions in the basal ganglia (putamen and caudate), thalami, and brainstem (periaqueductal grey, substantia nigra). MR spectroscopy may show an elevated lactate peak within the lesions. This pattern, combined with the clinical features (developmental regression, movement disorder, nystagmus), elevated blood and CSF lactate with a high lactate-to-pyruvate ratio, and maternal inheritance pattern, makes a clinical diagnosis of Leigh syndrome. The imaging pattern guides subsequent genetic testing. (Source: RCPCH: Mitochondrial Disease; GeneReviews: Leigh Syndrome)

explanation.summary: Neonatal hyperammonaemia is a metabolic emergency. The most common causes include urea cycle defects and organic acidaemias. The immediate management priority is to halt catabolism by ceasing protein-containing feeds and providing high-rate IV glucose. Definitive ammonia clearance via haemodialysis should be arranged in parallel when ammonia exceeds 400-500 micromol/L, but the first action is always metabolic stabilisation. Consanguinity raises the pre-test probability of autosomal recessive metabolic disorders.
key_points: Hyperammonaemia >200 micromol/L in a neonate is a metabolic emergency requiring immediate intervention
Cease all protein intake and provide IV 10% dextrose at 1.5x maintenance to suppress catabolism
Haemodialysis is the most efficient ammonia removal method but requires specialist setup
Normal CRP and absence of risk factors for sepsis shift the differential towards inborn errors of metabolism
Newborn screening may not detect all urea cycle defects and results may not yet be available at day 5
explanation.pearls: Ammonia levels above 400 micromol/L in neonates warrant haemodialysis referral, but the first bedside action is always cessation of protein plus IV dextrose - this can be done within minutes while organising dialysis access.

options.rationale: In suspected urea cycle defects or organic acidaemias presenting with hyperammonaemia, the immediate priority is to halt protein catabolism by ceasing enteral feeds (the protein source) and providing high-rate IV dextrose to suppress catabolism and provide energy substrate. This buys time while awaiting specialist metabolic input and definitive investigations. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperammonaemia)

Sodium bicarbonate corrects the acidosis symptomatically but does not address the underlying cause of hyperammonaemia. Ammonia continues to rise if protein catabolism is not halted. Bicarbonate may also cause paradoxical CNS acidosis and sodium load. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperammonaemia)

Neonatal sepsis is a reasonable differential for an unwell neonate, and empiric antibiotics may be given alongside metabolic management. However, the markedly elevated ammonia (680 micromol/L) with a normal CRP, consanguinity, and high anion gap acidosis point strongly to a metabolic disorder. Antibiotics do not address the ammonia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Haemodialysis is the most effective method of ammonia removal and is indicated when ammonia exceeds approximately 400-500 micromol/L depending on trajectory. However, it requires specialist setup and is not the initial management step - cessation of protein and IV glucose must begin immediately while dialysis is being arranged. (Source: JIMD Reports)

Sodium benzoate is an ammonia scavenger used in urea cycle defects, but it is given IV (not orally) in acute decompensation, and it is a secondary intervention after the immediate step of stopping protein intake and providing glucose. Oral administration in a vomiting neonate is also impractical. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperammonaemia)

explanation.summary: Complex febrile seizures are defined by focal features, duration greater than 15 minutes, or recurrence within 24 hours. In children under 18 months, signs of meningitis are unreliable, so the threshold for lumbar puncture should be low when complex features are present. The bilateral dull tympanic membranes suggest otitis media as the fever source, but this does not exclude concurrent meningitis. Neuroimaging and EEG are not part of routine febrile seizure workup.
key_points: Complex febrile seizure features: focal, >15 min duration, recurrence within 24 hours, or post-ictal focal deficit
LP threshold is low in children <18 months with complex febrile seizures because meningism is unreliable
Antiepileptic prophylaxis is not indicated for febrile seizures
CT brain is only indicated if signs of raised ICP or persistent focal deficit
EEG is not useful in the acute febrile seizure setting
explanation.pearls: In children under 18 months with complex febrile seizures, perform LP even when the fontanelle is flat and there is no neck stiffness - meningeal signs are unreliable below this age and meningitis must be actively excluded.

options.rationale: Discharge would be appropriate for a simple febrile seizure in a child over 12 months. However, this seizure is complex (focal, lasting >15 minutes equivalent with the 8-minute duration plus time to termination). In a child under 18 months with complex features, further investigation including LP consideration is warranted before discharge. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizure)

This child has a complex febrile seizure (focal, prolonged) at age 14 months. In children under 18 months with complex febrile seizures, the threshold for LP should be low because meningism is unreliable at this age. The flat fontanelle and absence of raised ICP signs make LP safe. Waiting until the child is more alert is appropriate post-ictal management. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizure)

Antiepileptic prophylaxis is not indicated after febrile seizures, even complex ones. Febrile seizures do not constitute epilepsy and long-term antiepileptics carry side-effect risk that outweighs the modest recurrence reduction. Intermittent oral diazepam during febrile illnesses may be discussed for frequent recurrences. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizure)

CT brain is not routinely indicated for febrile seizures, even complex ones, unless there are signs of raised intracranial pressure, persistent focal deficit, or clinical suspicion of an intracranial pathology. This child has a flat fontanelle and no focal signs post-ictally. CT would delay more important investigations. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizure)

EEG is not recommended acutely after febrile seizures. Post-ictal EEG findings are non-specific and do not reliably predict epilepsy risk. EEG may be considered if there are recurrent complex febrile seizures or afebrile seizures subsequently, but it is not part of the acute assessment. (Source: NICE CG176: Fever in Under 5s)

explanation.summary: Childhood absence epilepsy is characterised by frequent brief absence seizures with 3 Hz spike-and-wave on EEG. Ethosuximide is first-line, particularly in females, as it avoids valproate teratogenicity while maintaining equivalent efficacy. Sodium valproate remains an option if generalised tonic-clonic seizures coexist but should be avoided in girls where possible. Carbamazepine and phenytoin are contraindicated as they worsen absences. The prognosis is good, with approximately 70% of children achieving remission by adolescence.
key_points: Ethosuximide is first-line for childhood absence epilepsy, especially in females
Carbamazepine is contraindicated in absence epilepsy and can worsen seizures
Valproate is effective but avoided first-line in females due to teratogenicity
3 Hz generalised spike-and-wave on EEG provoked by hyperventilation is the classic finding
Lamotrigine is second-line but requires slow titration and is less effective for absences
explanation.pearls: Carbamazepine and phenytoin - both sodium channel blockers - can paradoxically worsen absence epilepsy and even trigger absence status epilepticus; always confirm the epilepsy syndrome before prescribing.

options.rationale: Carbamazepine is contraindicated in absence epilepsy as it can worsen absence seizures and may precipitate absence status epilepticus. It acts on sodium channels and is ineffective against the thalamocortical T-type calcium channel mechanism underlying absences. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Sodium valproate is effective for absence epilepsy and was historically first-line. However, in girls and women of childbearing potential, valproate carries significant teratogenic risk and should be avoided as first-line where alternatives exist. Australian and international guidelines now recommend ethosuximide for pure absence epilepsy in females. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Ethosuximide is first-line for childhood absence epilepsy, particularly in females given the teratogenicity concerns with valproate. It specifically targets T-type calcium channels in the thalamocortical circuit responsible for absence seizures. The SANAD II trial confirmed equivalent efficacy to valproate for absence epilepsy with a better side-effect profile. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Lamotrigine is a reasonable second-line option for absence epilepsy and avoids valproate teratogenicity concerns. However, it is less effective than ethosuximide for absence seizures as monotherapy and requires very slow titration over weeks to months due to the risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome, making it unsuitable as first choice. (Source: ILAE Treatment Guidelines)

Levetiracetam is broadly used in paediatric epilepsy but has limited evidence for absence seizures specifically. It is not recommended as first-line for childhood absence epilepsy by Australian or ILAE guidelines. Its mechanism does not target the T-type calcium channels involved in absence seizure generation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Macrophage activation syndrome is a life-threatening complication of systemic JIA, representing a form of secondary haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. The diagnostic hallmark is a paradoxically falling ESR (due to fibrinogen consumption) with markedly rising ferritin, in the context of cytopenias, hepatic dysfunction, and coagulopathy. First-line treatment is high-dose IV corticosteroids, with ciclosporin added for refractory cases. The HLH-2004 etoposide-based protocol is reserved for primary HLH or MAS not responding to steroids and ciclosporin.
key_points: Falling ESR with rising CRP and ferritin is the hallmark of MAS - ESR drops because fibrinogen is consumed
Ferritin above 10,000 microg/L in a child with sJIA should trigger immediate investigation for MAS
First-line treatment is IV methylprednisolone pulse therapy
Ciclosporin is second-line for steroid-refractory MAS
MAS can be triggered by infections, medication changes, or disease flares in sJIA
explanation.pearls: A falling ESR in a child with sJIA who is clinically deteriorating is a red flag for MAS - the ESR drops because fibrinogen is being consumed by disseminated intravascular coagulation, not because the disease is improving.

options.rationale: Methotrexate is a disease-modifying agent for JIA maintenance but is ineffective for acute macrophage activation syndrome (MAS). It also suppresses bone marrow and could worsen the cytopenias. MAS is an emergency requiring rapid immunosuppression with different agents. (Source: RCH CPG: Macrophage Activation Syndrome)

The presentation overlaps with severe sepsis - fever, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly, coagulopathy. However, the paradoxically falling ESR (8, previously 65) with rising CRP, massively elevated ferritin (>10,000), low fibrinogen, and hypertriglyceridaemia in a child with sJIA are diagnostic of MAS. Antibiotics alone do not treat the underlying hyperinflammatory state. (Source: RCH CPG: Macrophage Activation Syndrome)

Plasmapheresis may be considered as a rescue therapy in refractory MAS or haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), but it is not the initial treatment. First-line therapy for MAS complicating sJIA is high-dose corticosteroids, with ciclosporin added if refractory. Plasmapheresis requires central access and specialist support. (Source: Histiocyte Society HLH-2004 Protocol)

Etoposide-based HLH protocols (HLH-94/2004) are used for primary HLH and refractory secondary HLH. MAS complicating sJIA typically responds well to high-dose corticosteroids and ciclosporin, and etoposide carries significant toxicity including myelosuppression. It would only be considered if first-line MAS treatment fails. (Source: Histiocyte Society HLH-2004 Protocol)

High-dose IV methylprednisolone (pulse dosing up to 30 mg/kg/day, max 1 g) is the first-line treatment for MAS complicating sJIA. The falling ESR with rising CRP and ferritin is a hallmark of MAS - the ESR falls because fibrinogen (an acute phase reactant and ESR determinant) is consumed by the coagulopathy. Ciclosporin is added if there is no response within 24-48 hours. (Source: RCH CPG: Macrophage Activation Syndrome)

explanation.summary: Spiral fractures in pre-mobile infants are highly suspicious for non-accidental injury, particularly when the reported mechanism is inconsistent or biomechanically implausible. A 4-month-old cannot generate the rotational force required for a spiral humeral fracture by rolling off a couch. Mandatory reporting is a legal obligation for doctors across all Australian jurisdictions when there is reasonable suspicion of abuse. Investigation for organic causes (skeletal survey, bloods) and fracture treatment proceed in parallel with child protection involvement.
key_points: Spiral long-bone fractures in pre-mobile infants are highly suspicious for non-accidental injury
Mandatory notification to child protection occurs as soon as reasonable suspicion exists
A skeletal survey should be performed but notification should not wait for results
Inconsistent or biomechanically implausible mechanisms raise the index of suspicion
Investigation for organic causes (osteogenesis imperfecta, metabolic bone disease) occurs in parallel with notification
explanation.pearls: The humeral shaft is the most common long-bone fracture site in physical child abuse in infants under 12 months - a spiral or oblique pattern in a pre-mobile child has a positive predictive value for abuse exceeding 80%.

options.rationale: A spiral humeral fracture in a pre-mobile 4-month-old infant with an inconsistent and implausible mechanism (4-month-olds cannot roll off couches with enough force for a spiral humeral fracture) raises a high index of suspicion for non-accidental injury. All Australian states and territories have mandatory reporting legislation requiring notification. A skeletal survey and further workup should follow, but notification must not be delayed. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

Fracture management is necessary but does not address the child protection concern. Treating the fracture and discharging the infant without notification places the child at risk of further harm. Orthopaedic management occurs in parallel with child protection assessment, not instead of it. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

A skeletal survey is an important part of the non-accidental injury workup and may reveal occult fractures of different ages. However, waiting for the skeletal survey before notifying child protection is inappropriate - notification should occur as soon as reasonable suspicion exists, and a spiral fracture in a pre-mobile infant with inconsistent history meets that threshold. (Source: NSW Health: Mandatory Reporting)

Metabolic bone disease (e.g. osteogenesis imperfecta) and coagulopathy should be considered in the differential for unexplained fractures. However, these are uncommon and do not negate the obligation to notify child protection when the clinical picture is suspicious. Investigation for organic causes and child protection notification should occur in parallel. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

Admission and social work involvement are appropriate adjuncts but are not substitutes for mandatory notification to the statutory child protection authority. Social workers can support the family and assist with the process, but the doctor has a legal obligation to notify directly. Delaying notification pending social work review risks the child's safety. (Source: NSW Health: Mandatory Reporting)

explanation.summary: The Kocher criteria help distinguish septic arthritis from transient synovitis in children presenting with hip pain and effusion. The four criteria are: fever above 38.5, non-weight-bearing, WCC above 12 x10^9/L, and ESR above 40 mm/hr. With 3 or 4 criteria met, the probability of septic arthritis exceeds 90% and urgent joint aspiration is indicated. Staphylococcus aureus is the most common organism in this age group. Antibiotics should be withheld until after aspiration when possible, but not delayed if aspiration is impractical.
key_points: Kocher criteria: fever >38.5, non-weight-bearing, WCC >12, ESR >40 - three or more predicts >90% probability of septic arthritis
Joint aspiration is both diagnostic and therapeutic and should precede antibiotics when feasible
Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of septic arthritis in children
Transient synovitis typically follows viral illness but presents with lower or absent fever and normal inflammatory markers
CRP above 20 mg/L is a useful additional predictor (Caird modification of Kocher criteria)
explanation.pearls: Adding CRP above 20 mg/L to the original Kocher criteria (the Caird modification) improves specificity - a child meeting 4 of 5 modified criteria has a predicted probability of septic arthritis exceeding 98%.

options.rationale: This approach would be appropriate for transient synovitis, which typically follows viral illness in a well-looking child with low-grade or absent fever and normal inflammatory markers. This child has fever above 38.5, elevated CRP and WCC, and inability to bear weight - features that satisfy Kocher criteria for a high probability of septic arthritis. (Source: RCH CPG: Limping Child)

This child meets 3 of 4 Kocher criteria (fever >38.5, non-weight-bearing, WCC >12, ESR >40), giving a predicted probability of septic arthritis exceeding 90%. Joint aspiration is essential to confirm the diagnosis, identify the organism, and guide antibiotic therapy. The effusion confirmed on ultrasound makes aspiration technically feasible. (Source: RCH CPG: Limping Child)

Empiric antibiotics are necessary for septic arthritis but should ideally be given after joint aspiration to maximise the chance of identifying the causative organism. Starting antibiotics before obtaining synovial fluid reduces culture yield and may lead to prolonged empiric therapy. Aspiration also serves a therapeutic role by decompressing the joint. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

MRI can demonstrate joint effusion, synovial enhancement, and adjacent osteomyelitis, but it takes time to arrange, requires sedation in a 3-year-old, and delays definitive management. Ultrasound has already confirmed an effusion. Aspiration is both diagnostic and therapeutic and should not be delayed for MRI when the clinical picture is clear. (Source: RCH CPG: Limping Child)

Plain X-ray is part of the initial workup for a limping child and can exclude fracture or bony pathology. However, X-ray is insensitive for early septic arthritis - it may show soft tissue swelling or widened joint space but cannot distinguish septic arthritis from transient synovitis. Ultrasound has already demonstrated the effusion. Aspiration is the priority. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Septic Arthritis)

explanation.summary: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis is a common hip disorder of adolescence where the femoral head displaces posteriorly and inferiorly relative to the neck through the growth plate. Classic risk factors include obesity and male sex. The hallmark examination finding is obligate external rotation of the hip on flexion, with limited internal rotation. Knee pain is a common presenting complaint due to referred pain via the obturator nerve. Bilateral X-rays are essential as bilateral involvement occurs in up to 40% of cases.
key_points: Obligate external rotation on hip flexion with limited internal rotation is the hallmark of SUFE
Knee pain with normal knee examination in an adolescent should prompt hip examination
Bilateral AP and frog-leg lateral hip X-rays are the initial investigation of choice
Risk factors include obesity, male sex, adolescence, and endocrine disorders (hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency)
Up to 40% of SUFE cases have bilateral involvement - always image both hips
explanation.pearls: The frog-leg lateral view reveals early SUFE before it becomes visible on AP X-ray - Klein's line drawn along the superior femoral neck should intersect the lateral epiphysis; failure to do so (positive Trethowan sign) confirms the slip.

options.rationale: Knee pain in a child or adolescent with an unremarkable knee examination should prompt assessment of the hip, as referred pain from hip pathology is common via the obturator nerve. The normal knee examination and abnormal hip findings indicate the pathology is in the hip. An isolated knee X-ray would miss the diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Limping Child)

The clinical picture - obese adolescent male with insidious onset knee pain, obligate external rotation of the hip on flexion, and limited internal rotation - is classic for slipped upper femoral epiphysis (SUFE). Bilateral hip X-rays including frog-leg lateral views are essential, as the slip is often seen on the lateral view (Trethowan sign) and up to 40% of cases have bilateral involvement. (Source: RCH CPG: Limping Child)

MRI is sensitive for early SUFE and avascular necrosis but is not the initial investigation. Plain X-ray will confirm the diagnosis in most cases and is faster, cheaper, and does not require sedation. MRI may be indicated if X-ray is inconclusive in a pre-slip or early SUFE. (Source: POSNA: SCFE)

Hip ultrasound is useful for detecting effusion in younger children where transient synovitis or septic arthritis is suspected. In an afebrile obese 12-year-old with insidious onset symptoms and obligate external rotation, SUFE is far more likely than an inflammatory or infective process. Plain X-ray is the appropriate first-line investigation. (Source: RCH CPG: Limping Child)

Inflammatory markers are useful when septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, or inflammatory arthritis is suspected. This child is afebrile with a chronic insidious history and classic mechanical signs of SUFE. Blood tests would not contribute to the diagnosis and could delay appropriate imaging. (Source: RCH CPG: Limping Child)

explanation.summary: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis is classified as stable (able to weight-bear) or unstable (unable to weight-bear). Unstable SUFE carries a significantly higher rate of avascular necrosis (up to 47% vs 0-5% for stable). The treatment for both is in-situ fixation with a cannulated screw, but unstable SUFE requires urgent fixation. Reduction is avoided as it increases avascular necrosis risk. The contralateral hip should be monitored as prophylactic pinning is controversial but discussed in high-risk patients.
key_points: Unstable SUFE is defined by inability to weight-bear and carries up to 47% risk of avascular necrosis
Treatment is urgent in-situ screw fixation without reduction
Forced reduction increases avascular necrosis risk by disrupting retinacular blood supply
Traction is no longer recommended for SUFE management
Risk factors include obesity, endocrine disorders, and adolescence during the growth spurt
explanation.pearls: The Loder classification distinguishes stable (can weight-bear, even with crutches) from unstable (cannot weight-bear at all) SUFE - this single clinical distinction predicts avascular necrosis risk better than the degree of radiographic slip.

options.rationale: This is an acute-on-chronic unstable SUFE - the patient cannot weight-bear. Unstable SUFE carries a high risk of avascular necrosis of the femoral head (up to 47%), and any further displacement must be prevented. Weight-bearing is contraindicated and urgent surgical fixation is required. (Source: RCH CPG: SUFE)

Traction was historically used for SUFE but is no longer recommended as it does not prevent further displacement and may delay definitive fixation. Current guidelines recommend bed rest with no manipulation and urgent orthopaedic consultation for in-situ fixation within 24 hours. (Source: POSNA: SCFE)

Forced reduction of SUFE increases the risk of avascular necrosis by disrupting the remaining blood supply to the femoral head through the retinacular vessels. Current practice favours gentle in-situ fixation with a single cannulated screw rather than attempting to restore anatomy through reduction. (Source: RCH CPG: SUFE)

This is an acute-on-chronic unstable SUFE based on the inability to weight-bear, pre-existing symptoms, and radiographic findings. Management is strict non-weight-bearing (bed rest, stretcher transport) and urgent in-situ fixation with a single cannulated screw to prevent further displacement. The aim is to stabilise the epiphysis in its current position, not to reduce it. (Source: RCH CPG: SUFE)

MRI can assess femoral head perfusion and predict avascular necrosis risk, but it should not delay urgent surgical fixation. Each hour of delay increases the risk of further displacement and vascular compromise. MRI may be obtained post-fixation if avascular necrosis is suspected clinically. (Source: POSNA: SCFE)

explanation.summary: MCADD is an autosomal recessive disorder of mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation affecting approximately 1 in 10,000 live births. During fasting, the body cannot adequately oxidise medium-chain fatty acids for energy, leading to hypoketotic hypoglycaemia. The cardinal biochemical finding is inappropriately low ketones for the degree of hypoglycaemia. Newborn screening via tandem mass spectrometry detects elevated octanoylcarnitine (C8), but false negatives occur. Treatment is avoidance of prolonged fasting and emergency IV dextrose during illness.
key_points: Hypoketotic hypoglycaemia (low BSL with inappropriately low ketones) suggests a fatty acid oxidation disorder
MCADD is the most common fatty acid oxidation disorder, detectable on newborn screening
Presentation is typically during fasting stress from intercurrent illness in infancy or early childhood
Mild hepatic transaminase elevation occurs due to fatty infiltration during metabolic decompensation
Newborn screening is not 100% sensitive - clinical suspicion should prompt confirmatory acylcarnitine profile and genetic testing
explanation.pearls: The critical distinction is ketotic vs hypoketotic hypoglycaemia - when BSL is below 2.6 mmol/L, urinary ketones should be at least 2+ if fat oxidation pathways are intact; trace or absent ketones with severe hypoglycaemia mandates investigation for MCADD or hyperinsulinism.

options.rationale: Ketotic hypoglycaemia is the most common cause of hypoglycaemia in children aged 18 months to 5 years and characteristically presents with marked ketonuria during fasting. This child has hypoketotic hypoglycaemia (trace urinary ketones despite BSL 1.2), which is inconsistent with ketotic hypoglycaemia and suggests a fatty acid oxidation disorder. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

Congenital hyperinsulinism causes hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, which fits the biochemical picture. However, it typically presents in the neonatal period with persistent hypoglycaemia requiring high glucose infusion rates. Presentation at 11 months triggered specifically by fasting during illness, with normal inter-illness intervals, is more consistent with a fatty acid oxidation defect. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

Growth hormone deficiency can cause fasting hypoglycaemia in children, but it is typically accompanied by ketosis (as fat is mobilised but glucose production is impaired). The hypoketotic pattern and mildly elevated transaminases in this child point towards a fatty acid oxidation disorder rather than a hormone deficiency. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

Adrenal insufficiency can cause hypoglycaemia during physiological stress, but like growth hormone deficiency, it is associated with ketotic hypoglycaemia rather than hypoketotic. Electrolyte disturbances (hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia) would be expected in primary adrenal insufficiency, and the UEC is normal. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

MCADD is the most common fatty acid oxidation disorder and presents with hypoketotic hypoglycaemia during periods of fasting or metabolic stress. The hallmark is inappropriately low ketones for the degree of hypoglycaemia, mildly elevated transaminases from hepatic fat accumulation, and recurrent episodes triggered by intercurrent illness. Newborn screening detects most but not all cases. The history of recurrent fasting hypoglycaemia with trace ketones is classic. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

explanation.summary: Childhood ITP is an autoimmune condition causing isolated thrombocytopenia, typically following a viral illness. The platelet count alone does not dictate treatment - management is guided by bleeding severity. Skin-only manifestations (petechiae, bruising) without mucosal bleeding are managed with observation and activity restriction. Approximately 80% of childhood ITP resolves spontaneously within 6 months. Pharmacological treatment is reserved for significant mucosal bleeding, and IVIG is used for life-threatening haemorrhage.
key_points: ITP management is guided by bleeding severity, not platelet count alone
Skin-only ITP in a well child is managed with observation and activity restriction
Corticosteroids are reserved for significant mucosal bleeding in ITP
IVIG provides the fastest platelet rise and is used for severe or life-threatening bleeding
Platelet transfusion is generally ineffective in ITP due to autoimmune destruction
explanation.pearls: In childhood ITP, a platelet count of 8 x10^9/L with skin-only bleeding is managed with observation alone - the decision to treat is based on the severity of bleeding, not the number on the blood count.

options.rationale: This child has newly diagnosed immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) with skin-only bleeding (petechiae, bruising) and no mucosal haemorrhage. Despite the very low platelet count, current Australian and international guidelines recommend observation with activity restriction for ITP with skin-only manifestations, as spontaneous resolution occurs in approximately 80% of childhood ITP within 6 months. Treatment is reserved for significant mucosal bleeding. (Source: RCH CPG: ITP)

Oral prednisolone accelerates platelet recovery and is indicated in ITP with significant mucosal bleeding (epistaxis, gingival bleeding, haematuria) or when quality of life is significantly impaired. For skin-only manifestations in a well child, the side effects of corticosteroids (mood disturbance, weight gain, immunosuppression) outweigh the benefits. (Source: RCH CPG: ITP)

IVIG provides the fastest platelet rise (typically within 24-48 hours) and is indicated in ITP with life-threatening bleeding, significant mucosal haemorrhage, or when an urgent procedure is required. It is not first-line for skin-only ITP due to cost, infusion reactions, and the benign natural history of the condition. (Source: HSANZ: ITP Guidelines)

Platelet transfusion is generally avoided in ITP as the transfused platelets are rapidly destroyed by the same autoimmune mechanism. Platelet transfusion is reserved for life-threatening haemorrhage (intracranial, gastrointestinal) where temporising measures are needed. In skin-only ITP, platelet transfusion is not indicated. (Source: RCH CPG: ITP)

Bone marrow aspirate is not routinely required in typical childhood ITP presenting with isolated thrombocytopenia, normal white cell count and differential, and no hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. The blood film shows no blasts. Bone marrow aspirate is indicated if corticosteroids are to be commenced (to exclude leukaemia mimicking ITP) or if atypical features are present. (Source: RCH CPG: ITP)

explanation.summary: Incomplete Kawasaki disease is defined by fever for 5 or more days with fewer than 4 of the 5 classic clinical criteria, supported by laboratory abnormalities. It is more common in infants under 12 months, who are paradoxically at highest risk of coronary artery aneurysms. The laboratory features supporting the diagnosis include CRP above 30 mg/L, ESR above 40 mm/hr, hypoalbuminaemia, anaemia, thrombocytosis, elevated transaminases, and sterile pyuria. Treatment with IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin should not be delayed.
key_points: Incomplete Kawasaki: fever >=5 days with 2-3 classic criteria plus supportive lab findings
Infants under 12 months have the highest risk of coronary aneurysms and most commonly present incompletely
