IVIG 2 g/kg as a single infusion over 10-12 hours is the standard treatment
Sterile pyuria is a supportive laboratory finding for Kawasaki disease
Treatment within 10 days of fever onset reduces coronary aneurysm risk from 25% to approximately 4%
explanation.pearls: Sterile pyuria in Kawasaki disease results from urethral inflammation causing white cells in urine that is culture-negative - it occurs in up to 80% of cases and should not be mistaken for UTI.

options.rationale: This child has 6 days of fever with 2 of 5 classic Kawasaki criteria (conjunctival injection, lip changes), meeting the definition of incomplete Kawasaki disease. Infants under 12 months are at highest risk of coronary artery aneurysms and incomplete presentations are more common in this age group. Delaying treatment increases the risk of coronary involvement. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

Aspirin is part of Kawasaki management but is given alongside IVIG, not alone. Echocardiography should be performed urgently (not as an outpatient) given the 6 days of fever and high risk of coronary involvement in an infant. Aspirin monotherapy is insufficient to prevent coronary artery aneurysms. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

This infant meets criteria for incomplete Kawasaki disease: fever for 5 or more days with 2-3 classic features, plus supportive laboratory findings (CRP >30, ESR >40, albumin <30, anaemia, thrombocytosis, elevated ALT, sterile pyuria). In infants under 12 months with incomplete Kawasaki, the threshold for treatment should be low due to higher coronary risk. IVIG 2 g/kg over 10-12 hours plus high-dose aspirin is the standard treatment. Echocardiography assesses coronary arteries. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

Blood and urine cultures are negative, and the sterile pyuria is characteristic of Kawasaki disease rather than urinary tract infection. The clinical picture with prolonged fever, conjunctival injection, lip changes, and supportive laboratories is more consistent with Kawasaki disease than occult bacterial infection. Antibiotics would not prevent coronary artery aneurysms. (Source: AHA Kawasaki Disease Guidelines)

CT angiography is not the initial cardiac investigation in suspected Kawasaki disease. Transthoracic echocardiography is the standard imaging modality for assessing coronary artery dimensions in children. CT carries radiation exposure and typically requires sedation. It may be used later for detailed follow-up of known aneurysms. (Source: AHA Kawasaki Disease Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency is the most common cause of congenital adrenal hyperplasia, accounting for over 90% of cases. Salt-wasting forms present at 1-3 weeks of life with adrenal crisis characterised by hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, metabolic acidosis, and circulatory collapse. Female infants are typically diagnosed earlier due to virilised genitalia at birth, but male infants have normal external genitalia and are often only diagnosed at salt-wasting crisis. Newborn screening detects elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone but results may not be available before presentation.
key_points: Salt-wasting CAH typically presents at 1-3 weeks of life as mineralocorticoid reserves are depleted
Male infants with CAH have normal external genitalia and are diagnosed later than females
The electrolyte triad of hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, and hypoglycaemia with metabolic acidosis is characteristic
Hyperpigmentation from ACTH excess may be present from birth
Emergency treatment is IV 0.9% NaCl, IV dextrose, and IV hydrocortisone 25 mg bolus
explanation.pearls: Male infants with salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency present on average 5-7 days later than females because their normal external genitalia do not trigger earlier investigation - the salt-wasting crisis at day 10-21 is often the first clinical clue.

options.rationale: This male neonate presents in salt-wasting adrenal crisis at day 16 - the classic timing for 21-hydroxylase deficiency. The combination of hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, metabolic acidosis, and shock is pathognomonic for mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid deficiency. Hyperpigmentation from ACTH excess supports the diagnosis. Male infants with classic CAH have normal genitalia, so the diagnosis is often missed until salt-wasting crisis at 1-3 weeks of life. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia)

Neonatal sepsis can cause shock with electrolyte derangement, but the specific pattern of hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia is more consistent with primary adrenal insufficiency than sepsis-related adrenal suppression. Sepsis typically causes hyponatraemia without hyperkalaemia, and the hyperpigmentation present from birth suggests a congenital rather than acquired process. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia)

Pyloric stenosis presents with projectile vomiting at 2-6 weeks of age but causes hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis from gastric acid loss - the opposite electrolyte pattern to this case. This infant has metabolic acidosis with hyperkalaemia, which is inconsistent with pyloric stenosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

Type 4 renal tubular acidosis can cause hyperkalaemic metabolic acidosis, but it does not explain the severe hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia, or shock in this presentation. The combination of all four features (hypoNa, hyperK, hypo BSL, shock) at day 16 of life with hyperpigmentation is far more consistent with congenital adrenal hyperplasia. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia)

Duct-dependent congenital heart disease can present with shock in the first weeks of life as the ductus arteriosus closes. However, it does not cause the specific electrolyte pattern of hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia. Cardiogenic shock would typically present with hepatomegaly, tachypnoea, and differential saturations rather than this metabolic picture. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease)

explanation.summary: Intussusception is the most common cause of bowel obstruction in infants aged 3 months to 3 years. The classic triad of colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, and red currant jelly stool is present in only 20-40% of cases. Inter-episode lethargy is an important and often underappreciated feature. Abdominal ultrasound is the investigation of choice with near-perfect sensitivity. Treatment is air or hydrostatic enema reduction, with surgical intervention reserved for failed reduction or perforation.
key_points: Abdominal ultrasound has sensitivity >98% for intussusception and is the first-line investigation
The classic triad (colicky pain, vomiting, red currant jelly stool) is present in only 20-40% of cases
Inter-episode lethargy or pallor may be the dominant feature and should raise suspicion
Air enema reduction has a success rate of 80-95% for ileocolic intussusception
Preceding viral illness is a common trigger via mesenteric lymphoid hyperplasia
explanation.pearls: Inter-episode lethargy in an infant with episodic distress is a red flag for intussusception - up to 30% of cases present with altered consciousness as the dominant feature, sometimes without obvious abdominal pain.

options.rationale: Plain abdominal X-ray has poor sensitivity (approximately 50%) for intussusception. It may show a soft tissue mass, meniscus sign, or absent caecal gas, but a normal X-ray does not exclude the diagnosis. Ultrasound is the investigation of choice with sensitivity exceeding 98%. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

CT is not the first-line investigation for suspected intussusception in a paediatric patient. It involves significant radiation exposure and typically requires sedation in an infant. Abdominal ultrasound provides superior diagnostic accuracy for intussusception without radiation. CT may be used if complications are suspected (e.g. perforation). (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

Abdominal ultrasound is the gold-standard investigation for intussusception with sensitivity of 98-100% and specificity of 88-100%. The classic finding is the target sign (or doughnut sign) on transverse view, representing the layers of intussuscepted bowel. This child has a classic presentation: episodic colicky pain with drawing up of knees, inter-episode lethargy, and red currant jelly stool. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

Air enema is both diagnostic and therapeutic for ileocolic intussusception and has a reduction success rate of approximately 80-95%. However, it should be preceded by ultrasound confirmation to avoid unnecessary intervention. Air enema also carries risks of perforation and should be performed by an experienced radiologist with surgical standby. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

The preceding viral gastroenteritis is a common antecedent to intussusception (via mesenteric lymphoid hyperplasia acting as a lead point), but identifying the specific virus does not change management. The priority is diagnosing and treating the intussusception, not characterising the preceding infection. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Intussusception)

explanation.summary: Paediatric DKA fluid management differs significantly from adult protocols due to the risk of cerebral oedema. Fluid deficit is estimated at 5% for moderate and 7% for severe DKA and is replaced evenly over 48 hours using isotonic saline. Insulin infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/hr is commenced 1 hour after starting IV fluids. Blood glucose should not fall faster than 5 mmol/L/hr. When BSL reaches 15-17 mmol/L, glucose is added to the fluid to allow continued insulin infusion for ketone clearance.
key_points: Paediatric DKA fluid deficit is replaced over 48 hours to reduce cerebral oedema risk
0.9% NaCl is used initially - not hypotonic fluids
Insulin at 0.1 unit/kg/hr is started 1 hour after commencing IV fluids
Blood glucose target fall rate is no more than 5 mmol/L/hr
Add 5% dextrose to IV fluids when BSL reaches 15-17 mmol/L to allow continued insulin for ketone clearance
explanation.pearls: The corrected sodium should rise as blood glucose falls during DKA treatment - a falling corrected sodium is a warning sign for developing cerebral oedema and warrants immediate reassessment of fluid rate and consideration of hypertonic saline or mannitol.

options.rationale: A fluid rate of 5 mL/kg/hr is excessive for paediatric DKA and increases the risk of cerebral oedema. Australian guidelines (ISPAD/RCH) recommend calculating total fluid replacement over 48 hours using maintenance plus deficit (estimated at 5-7% dehydration), with deficit replaced evenly over 48 hours. Insulin at 0.1 unit/kg/hr is correct. (Source: RCH CPG: DKA)

This fluid strategy is close to correct but the insulin dose of 0.05 unit/kg/hr is below the standard starting rate. ISPAD guidelines recommend starting at 0.1 unit/kg/hr for paediatric DKA. A rate of 0.05 unit/kg/hr may be used for younger children or if blood glucose falls too rapidly, but it is not the standard starting dose. (Source: RCH CPG: DKA)

This follows Australian and ISPAD paediatric DKA guidelines. Fluid is calculated as maintenance plus estimated deficit (5% for moderate DKA based on pH 7.12 and clinical assessment) replaced evenly over 48 hours. Insulin infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/hr is commenced 1 hour after starting IV fluids to avoid rapid osmotic shifts. The slower rehydration over 48 hours reduces the risk of cerebral oedema compared to more aggressive regimens. (Source: RCH CPG: DKA)

Hypotonic fluids (0.45% NaCl) should not be used in the initial phase of paediatric DKA management as they can exacerbate cerebral oedema by increasing the osmotic gradient. Isotonic 0.9% NaCl is used initially. Starting insulin immediately after the bolus without the recommended 1-hour fluid-first period may cause rapid glucose and osmolality shifts. (Source: RCH CPG: DKA)

Replacing the deficit over 24 hours rather than 48 hours is too rapid for paediatric DKA. Rapid fluid administration increases the risk of cerebral oedema, which is the leading cause of DKA-related mortality in children. Australian and ISPAD guidelines specifically recommend deficit replacement over 48 hours. (Source: ISPAD DKA Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Typical (STEC-associated) haemolytic uraemic syndrome is the most common cause of acute kidney injury in young children. It follows diarrhoeal illness caused by Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, most commonly O157:H7. The triad is microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury. Antibiotics are specifically contraindicated as they increase Shiga toxin release and may worsen the disease. Management is supportive with careful fluid balance, blood transfusion as needed, and dialysis for severe AKI.
key_points: Antibiotics are contraindicated in STEC infection - they increase Shiga toxin release and may worsen HUS
The classic triad is microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and AKI
Schistocytes on blood film confirm microangiopathic haemolysis
Platelet transfusion is relatively contraindicated as it may fuel the thrombotic microangiopathy
50-70% of children with STEC-HUS require dialysis during the acute phase
explanation.pearls: Antibiotic administration during STEC infection increases the risk of developing HUS by 14-17 fold - the SOS response triggered by antibiotics (especially fluoroquinolones and trimethoprim) upregulates Shiga toxin production and release from dying bacteria.

options.rationale: Platelet transfusion is relatively contraindicated in typical HUS as it may fuel the thrombotic microangiopathy by providing substrate for further microvascular thrombosis. However, it may be given for active life-threatening bleeding or before invasive procedures. While it should be avoided if possible, it is not the most specifically contraindicated intervention. (Source: RCH CPG: HUS)

Red cell transfusion is appropriate and recommended in HUS when haemoglobin falls below 60-70 g/L or the patient is symptomatic. Unlike platelet transfusion, packed red cells do not contribute to the thrombotic microangiopathy. Transfusion should be given slowly to avoid fluid overload in the setting of renal failure. (Source: RCH CPG: HUS)

Careful IV fluid management is essential in HUS. Early volume expansion may reduce the severity of renal injury. However, fluid must be carefully titrated in the setting of oliguria and hypertension to avoid fluid overload. Isotonic crystalloid is appropriate for initial resuscitation. (Source: RCH CPG: HUS)

Antibiotics are specifically contraindicated in Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC) infection complicated by or at risk of HUS. Antibiotic-mediated bacterial lysis releases additional Shiga toxin, which may worsen the thrombotic microangiopathy and increase the risk of progression to HUS or worsening of established HUS. This is one of the few infections where antibiotics are actively harmful. (Source: RCH CPG: HUS)

Renal replacement therapy (dialysis) is indicated in HUS for severe or refractory AKI with complications such as refractory hyperkalaemia, fluid overload, or uraemic encephalopathy. It is an important part of supportive management and should not be avoided. Approximately 50-70% of children with STEC-HUS require dialysis during the acute phase. (Source: RCH CPG: HUS)

explanation.summary: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis classically presents in first-born males at 3-6 weeks with progressive projectile non-bilious vomiting. The pathognomonic metabolic derangement is hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis from gastric acid loss. Pyloromyotomy is curative but is never an emergency - the metabolic abnormalities must be corrected first. IV 0.9% NaCl with potassium supplementation is the resuscitation fluid of choice. Surgery should only proceed once chloride exceeds 100 mmol/L and bicarbonate is below 26 mmol/L.
key_points: Pyloric stenosis causes hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis from HCl loss in vomit
Pyloromyotomy is not an emergency - correct the metabolic derangement before surgery
IV 0.9% NaCl with KCl is the resuscitation fluid - replaces chloride and potassium
Surgical readiness targets: chloride >100 mmol/L, bicarbonate <26 mmol/L, potassium >3.5 mmol/L
Respiratory compensation for metabolic alkalosis is hypoventilation - which risks apnoea under anaesthesia
explanation.pearls: The kidneys initially compensate for the alkalosis by excreting bicarbonate in urine (alkaline urine), but as volume depletion worsens, the kidneys prioritise sodium reabsorption over acid-base correction, producing the paradoxical aciduria of pyloric stenosis.

options.rationale: This infant has a metabolic alkalosis (pH 7.52, HCO3 38), not acidosis. The elevated pCO2 represents respiratory compensation (hypoventilation to retain CO2). Pyloric stenosis causes loss of gastric hydrochloric acid through vomiting, producing hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Identifying the correct acid-base disturbance is essential for pre-operative correction. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

The blood results do not show thrombocytopenia. Pyloric stenosis does not cause thrombocytopenia. The key pre-operative concern is the metabolic alkalosis with hypokalaemia and hypochloraemia, which must be corrected with IV 0.9% NaCl with KCl supplementation before safe anaesthesia. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

The sodium is 133 mmol/L, which is low-normal to mildly hyponatraemic, not hypernatraemic. Pyloric stenosis typically causes hyponatraemia from volume depletion and aldosterone-mediated sodium retention being overwhelmed by losses. The key correction needed is the metabolic alkalosis, hypochloraemia, and hypokalaemia. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

While infants with pyloric stenosis can develop hypoglycaemia from poor oral intake, the investigations provided do not include a BSL result indicating hypoglycaemia. The critical pre-operative correction in pyloric stenosis is the electrolyte and acid-base disturbance - specifically the hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

Pyloric stenosis causes loss of gastric HCl, producing hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. This must be corrected before anaesthesia because alkalosis shifts the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve leftward (impairing tissue oxygen delivery), hypokalaemia predisposes to cardiac arrhythmias under anaesthesia, and compensatory hypoventilation may cause apnoea during induction. Correction is achieved with IV 0.9% NaCl plus KCl supplementation over 24-48 hours. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

explanation.summary: New-onset ataxia in a child requires neuroimaging to exclude posterior fossa tumours, which are the most common solid tumours of childhood. Post-varicella acute cerebellar ataxia is the most common cause of acute ataxia in preschool children and typically presents 1-2 weeks after varicella infection. It is a diagnosis of exclusion - MRI must be performed before the diagnosis is made. Post-infectious cerebellar ataxia is self-limiting, with most children recovering completely within 2-4 weeks.
key_points: MRI brain is mandatory for any child with new-onset ataxia to exclude posterior fossa tumour
Post-varicella cerebellar ataxia is immune-mediated, not active infection - aciclovir is not helpful
Red flags for posterior fossa tumour: persistent headache, morning vomiting, papilloedema, cranial nerve palsies
Posterior fossa tumours (medulloblastoma, astrocytoma, ependymoma) are the most common solid tumours of childhood
Post-infectious cerebellar ataxia is self-limiting with recovery in 2-4 weeks in most cases
explanation.pearls: Post-varicella cerebellar ataxia occurs in approximately 1 in 4,000 cases of childhood varicella and typically appears 1-2 weeks after the rash - the incidence has declined significantly since routine varicella vaccination was added to the Australian National Immunisation Program in 2005.

options.rationale: While post-infectious (post-varicella) acute cerebellar ataxia is the most likely diagnosis given the recent chickenpox and absence of red flag features, it is a diagnosis of exclusion. An MRI brain must be performed to exclude a posterior fossa tumour before this diagnosis can be made with confidence. Posterior fossa tumours can present identically in this age group. (Source: RCH CPG: Ataxia)

Post-varicella cerebellar ataxia is an immune-mediated process, not active viral infection of the cerebellum. It occurs 1-2 weeks after the primary infection and is thought to result from cross-reactive antibodies or T-cell responses against cerebellar antigens. Aciclovir does not treat the ataxia. If varicella encephalitis were suspected (altered consciousness, seizures), aciclovir would be indicated, but this child is alert and well. (Source: RCH CPG: Ataxia)

Corticosteroids are not routinely recommended for acute post-infectious cerebellar ataxia, which is typically self-limiting with resolution over days to weeks. If a more severe acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM) pattern were identified on MRI, corticosteroids might be indicated. Empiric steroids before imaging could also mask or complicate interpretation of a posterior fossa tumour. (Source: RCH CPG: Ataxia)

In any child presenting with new-onset ataxia, MRI brain is essential to exclude a posterior fossa tumour (medulloblastoma, astrocytoma, ependymoma) before attributing symptoms to a benign post-infectious aetiology. Posterior fossa tumours are the most common solid tumours of childhood and present with ataxia in this age group. The absence of headache, vomiting, papilloedema, and cranial nerve signs makes tumour less likely but does not exclude it. (Source: RCH CPG: Ataxia)

The child is afebrile, alert, interactive, and has no meningism or encephalopathic features. Lumbar puncture is not the priority investigation. While CSF analysis can support a diagnosis of post-infectious cerebellitis (mild pleocytosis), the critical investigation is MRI to exclude a structural cause. LP may be considered after imaging if the clinical picture is unclear. (Source: RCH CPG: Ataxia)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis escalation in Australian paediatric units follows a stepwise model: minimal handling and nasogastric or IV fluids, supplemental oxygen, HFNC for SpO2 under 92 percent or moderate work of breathing, then NIV or intubation for HFNC failure. HFNC failure is defined by persistent SpO2 under 90 percent at FiO2 above 0.4, rising pCO2 above 60 mmHg, or recurrent apnoeas. NIV with PEEP 5 to 7 cmH2O is the next step before intubation in most centres. PICU contact is mandatory at the point of HFNC failure.
key_points: HFNC failure criteria: FiO2 over 0.4 with SpO2 under 90 percent, pCO2 over 60 mmHg, or apnoeas
Salbutamol and adrenaline are not recommended in infants under 12 months with bronchiolitis
Apnoeas are typical of RSV in infants under 3 months and warrant high-acuity observation
Escalate to NIV before intubation when criteria met; involve PICU early
explanation.pearls: In an infant under 3 months on HFNC at 2 L/kg/min with FiO2 above 0.4 and any apnoea within 30 minutes, escalate to NIV that hour - do not retry HFNC settings.

options.rationale: Persistent hypercapnia, falling saturations and recurrent apnoeas on established HFNC define HFNC failure; further passive observation risks respiratory arrest. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

Nebulised adrenaline has not been shown to alter the natural history of bronchiolitis and does not address the apnoeas or hypercapnia driving deterioration here. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis; PREDICT bronchiolitis guideline)

Imaging beyond the existing chest X-ray will not change acute management; the priority is ventilatory support, and apnoeas in RSV infants are characteristic and do not need ID review. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
Beta-2 agonists are not recommended in bronchiolitis under 12 months; salbutamol risks tachycardia and lactataemia without bronchodilator response in this age group. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

HFNC failure (rising pCO2, apnoeas, persistent saturations under 90%) in an infant under 3 months meets escalation criteria; NIV with PEEP recruits collapsed alveoli and PICU transfer secures airway support. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis; ANZICS paediatric NIV)

explanation.summary:
Continuous or back-to-back beta-2 agonist therapy predictably causes hypokalaemia, lactataemia, tremor and tachycardia. These are drug effects, not markers of worsening asthma, and the correct response in a child who is clinically improving is to replace potassium and keep the bronchodilator going. Potassium is added to the intravenous fluid with cardiac monitoring and the level rechecked. Stopping the salbutamol in order to normalise the biochemistry trades a treatable electrolyte problem for a treatable airway problem.

In context: acute asthma in children is managed by severity. Inhaled salbutamol with a spacer or nebuliser, ipratropium for severe episodes, and systemic corticosteroid within the first hour are the core of treatment, with intravenous magnesium sulfate then intravenous salbutamol for children failing maximal inhaled therapy. Monitoring during this escalation covers work of breathing, oxygenation, potassium, glucose and lactate, and the commonest error at this point is to misread the pharmacology of the drug as deterioration of the disease.
key_points: Hypokalaemia, lactataemia and tremor are expected beta-2 agonist effects
Replace potassium and continue salbutamol in a child who is improving
Lactate rising on salbutamol is not evidence of sepsis
Recheck potassium and keep the child on cardiac monitoring
explanation.pearls: The child who is getting better clinically but whose numbers are getting uglier is usually showing you the drug, not the disease.

options.rationale: Beta-2 agonists drive potassium intracellularly and generate lactate; both are expected pharmacological effects in a child responding clinically. The RCH acute asthma guideline advises monitoring and replacing potassium rather than withdrawing the bronchodilator that is working. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute; AMH Children's Dosing Companion)

Magnesium replaces nothing here. It would be right if the child were failing maximal inhaled therapy with persistent severe work of breathing, which is the RCH trigger for the first intravenous bronchodilator. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

Bicarbonate is reserved for severe metabolic acidosis with haemodynamic compromise, such as established shock or a toxic ingestion. Salbutamol lactataemia with a near normal pH does not warrant it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

Insulin and dextrose shift potassium into cells and would be right for dangerous hyperkalaemia with electrocardiographic change, the opposite disturbance to the one present. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute; AMH Children's Dosing Companion)

Watchful waiting suits a child with mild exacerbation and normal biochemistry. A potassium of 2.7 mmol/L with ongoing beta-2 agonist exposure risks arrhythmia and needs replacement now. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook)

explanation.summary: Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for moderate to severe croup and produces transient bronchospasm relief lasting about 2 hours. Australian guidelines require at least 3 hours of observation after the dose, ideally 4 hours, to capture rebound stridor. Dexamethasone is given concurrently and has onset over 2 to 6 hours, so observation also confirms steroid efficacy. Discharge criteria include stridor-free at rest, normal work of breathing, oral intake adequate, and reliable carers within travelling distance of a service.
key_points: Observe for 3 to 4 hours after nebulised adrenaline for rebound stridor
Dexamethasone 0.15 to 0.6 mg/kg PO is the standard steroid dose
Repeat adrenaline only if stridor returns - not prophylactically
Bacterial tracheitis or epiglottitis should be reconsidered if not responsive
explanation.pearls: A child who needs a second dose of nebulised adrenaline within the first 3 hours warrants admission and PICU notification, regardless of how well they look between doses.

options.rationale: Discharge before the post-adrenaline observation window risks rebound stridor at home; adrenaline effect is short and stridor can recur within hours. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

Australian guidelines require observation for 3 to 4 hours after nebulised adrenaline because the effect lasts approximately 2 hours and rebound stridor may occur; if stable at that point, discharge is safe. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup; eTG Paediatrics)
Mandatory admission overnight is not required if he remains stridor-free at rest 3 to 4 hours after adrenaline; admission decisions are clinical, not routine. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Repeat adrenaline is given only if stridor recurs; he is currently stridor-free and a routine repeat dose adds no benefit but obscures the observation window. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
A second dexamethasone dose is not standard within the same episode; the issue is observation length after adrenaline, not steroid dosing. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Australian paediatric CAP guidance recommends oral amoxicillin as first line for non-severe CAP in fully immunised children, 25 mg/kg three times daily (or twice daily formulation depending on preparation) for 5 days. Pneumococcus remains dominant despite vaccination, and amoxicillin has excellent pneumococcal coverage. Macrolides add atypical cover but atypicals are uncommon under 5 years. IV is reserved for severe disease (SpO2 under 92 percent persistent on oxygen, dehydration, failure of oral therapy). Add macrolide if atypical features (older child, dry cough, headache, gradual onset).
key_points: Amoxicillin 25 mg/kg TDS for 5 days for uncomplicated paediatric CAP
Atypicals are uncommon in under-5s; macrolide-first not indicated
IV penicillin only for severe disease or failure of oral
Add macrolide for atypical features (school age, dry cough, headache)
explanation.pearls: If a child fails 48 hours of oral amoxicillin for CAP, think effusion, empyema or atypical - re-image with ultrasound and add azithromycin only then.

options.rationale: Atypical organisms are uncommon causes of CAP in children under 5 years; macrolide-first treatment misses pneumococcal cover that remains the dominant pathogen. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic - paediatric pneumonia)

Broader gram-negative cover is not indicated for uncomplicated community-acquired pneumonia in an immunised, well-appearing toddler; clavulanate increases diarrhoea risk without benefit. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic - paediatric pneumonia)

Australian paediatric CAP guidelines recommend amoxicillin as the first-line agent because Streptococcus pneumoniae remains the dominant pathogen; 5 days is sufficient for uncomplicated cases. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic - paediatric pneumonia; AMH Children's Dosing Companion)

IV therapy is reserved for severe CAP, vomiting, or failure of oral therapy; she is feeding and not severely unwell, so oral amoxicillin is appropriate. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic - paediatric pneumonia)

Cefuroxime is not first-line for paediatric CAP in Australia; it has poor pneumococcal penetration at oral doses and broader spectrum is not warranted. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic - paediatric pneumonia)

explanation.summary: Incomplete Kawasaki disease is diagnosed on fever 5 or more days plus 2 or 3 classic features, supported by elevated inflammatory markers and at least 3 of: anaemia, platelets above 450 x10^9/L after day 7, albumin under 30 g/L, ALT elevation, WCC above 15 x10^9/L, sterile pyuria, or coronary changes on echo. IVIG 2 g/kg as a single infusion plus aspirin should be given within 10 days of fever onset to reduce coronary artery aneurysm risk from about 25 percent to under 5 percent. High-risk patients (under 1 year, Asian descent, low albumin, high CRP) may benefit from added corticosteroid (PUFA score 5 or above).
key_points: Treat incomplete Kawasaki on the algorithm - do not wait for 4 of 5 classic features
IVIG 2 g/kg single dose within 10 days of fever onset
Adjunct aspirin (anti-inflammatory then antiplatelet)
Echocardiogram at diagnosis, 2 weeks, 6 to 8 weeks
High-risk groups (under 1 year, Asian, high CRP) may need adjunct steroid
explanation.pearls: Sterile pyuria, ALT above 50 U/L, albumin under 30 g/L, and platelets above 450 x10^9/L after day 7 are the four lab criteria that move an incomplete picture into 'treat'.

options.rationale: Day 6 of fever above 39 degrees C with conjunctivitis, mucocutaneous features and a marked inflammatory profile is high risk; expectant management risks missing the IVIG window for coronary protection. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

Incomplete Kawasaki criteria (fever 5 or more days plus 2 to 3 classic features) with elevated CRP and other supportive labs (sterile pyuria, platelet rise, low albumin, raised ALT) meets the AHA/RCH algorithm for treatment; IVIG within 10 days protects coronary arteries. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease; AHA 2017 scientific statement)
He has no source of bacterial infection and is well perfused; empirical antibiotics are unlikely to be needed and delay specific therapy for Kawasaki. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)
Steroids may be added for high-risk Kawasaki or IVIG resistance but are not first-line monotherapy in Australian practice; IVIG remains the primary treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

Delaying treatment until day 10 increases coronary artery aneurysm risk; the algorithm explicitly supports treating incomplete cases earlier when labs and echo support the diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

explanation.summary: After a first typical febrile UTI in a child over 6 months with normal antenatal scans and good response to first-line antibiotics, the Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG does NOT recommend routine imaging. Imaging is triggered by ATYPICAL features (slow response, non-E coli organism, sepsis or septicaemia, abdominal mass, raised creatinine) or by RECURRENCE. Infants under 6 months get ultrasound if recurrent UTI or no antenatal monitoring. DMSA and MCUG are reserved for abnormal ultrasound, recurrent infection, suspected posterior urethral valves or marked hydronephrosis.
key_points: First typical febrile UTI in a well child over 6 months with normal antenatal scans - no routine imaging (RCH Melbourne CPG)
Ultrasound triggered by atypical UTI or recurrence, or by infants under 6 months with recurrent UTI or no antenatal scans
DMSA and MCUG are reserved for abnormal ultrasound, recurrent UTI, or suspected PUV
Counsel parents to present early for any future fever
explanation.pearls: Atypical UTI features per RCH Melbourne are: poor response to 48 hours of antibiotics, non-E coli organism, septicaemia, abdominal or bladder mass, raised creatinine, or recurrence - any one triggers ultrasound.

options.rationale: Routine renal tract ultrasound is not required after a first typical febrile UTI per the Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG. Ultrasound during the acute illness is recommended for atypical UTI (poor response, non-E coli organism, sepsis, abdominal mass, raised creatinine) and for infants under 6 months with recurrent UTI or no antenatal monitoring. This child had a typical UTI, defervesced in 48 hours, has normal antenatal scans, and is over 6 months old - imaging is not indicated. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG: Urinary Tract Infection)

MCUG and DMSA are reserved for recurrent UTI, atypical features, or abnormal renal tract ultrasound; both involve radiation and MCUG is invasive. Neither is indicated after a single typical UTI. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG: UTI)

DMSA is reserved for atypical or recurrent UTI, abnormal ultrasound or high suspicion of reflux nephropathy; a single typical UTI with good response does not require it. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG: UTI)
Routine antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended after a single uncomplicated febrile UTI in an otherwise well child. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG: UTI)

Per the Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG, no follow-up imaging is required after a first typical febrile UTI in a well child over 6 months with normal antenatal scans and good response to first-line antibiotics. Renal tract ultrasound is reserved for atypical UTI (poor response, non-E coli, sepsis, abdominal mass, raised creatinine), recurrent UTI, or infants under 6 months with recurrent UTI or absent antenatal monitoring. Counsel parents on prompt presentation for any future fever and arrange GP follow-up. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG: Urinary Tract Infection)

explanation.summary: Hospital-acquired hyponatraemia in children remains a recognised hazard of hypotonic maintenance fluids in the setting of stress-induced ADH release. Australian and international paediatric guidance now recommends isotonic maintenance (0.9 percent saline plus 5 percent dextrose) for most acutely unwell children. Symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizure, depressed conscious state) requires immediate 3 percent sodium chloride 2 to 5 mL/kg bolus. The aim is to raise serum sodium by 4 to 6 mmol/L acutely to resolve symptoms; thereafter correct slowly over 24 hours.
key_points: Use isotonic maintenance (0.9% NaCl + 5% glucose) in acutely unwell children
Symptomatic hyponatraemia: 3% NaCl 2 to 5 mL/kg bolus
Aim to raise Na by 4 to 6 mmol/L acutely to abort symptoms
Avoid raising Na by more than 8 to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours (osmotic demyelination)
Investigate cause (SIADH, gastro losses, water intoxication)
explanation.pearls: In an unwell child with hyponatraemic seizure, give 3% sodium chloride 2 mL/kg bolus and recheck the sodium in 15 minutes - the seizure stops almost immediately as Na rises 3 to 5 mmol/L.

options.rationale: Isotonic saline raises sodium too slowly in symptomatic hyponatraemia and large volumes risk further dilution if SIADH is contributing. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyponatraemia)
Benzodiazepine alone treats the seizure symptom but does not address the underlying acute hyponatraemia driving it; ongoing low sodium will re-seize. (Source: RCH CPG: Seizure)

Acute symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizure) requires immediate sodium correction with hypertonic 3 percent saline 2 to 5 mL/kg bolus; this raises serum sodium acutely to abort the seizure and reduce cerebral oedema. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyponatraemia; ANZICS)
Mannitol is not first line in hyponatraemic cerebral oedema; the driver is low effective osmolality and the answer is to raise sodium with hypertonic saline. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyponatraemia)
Phenytoin is a second-line anticonvulsant; in hyponatraemic seizure the priority is correcting sodium with hypertonic saline. (Source: RCH CPG: Seizure)

explanation.summary: A simple febrile seizure is generalised, lasts under 15 minutes, has no recurrence within 24 hours and occurs between 6 months and 5 years. In a fully immunised, alert child without signs of meningitis, lumbar puncture is not routine. LP is indicated for signs of meningitis (bulging fontanelle, neck stiffness, persistent altered mental state), complex febrile seizure (focal, prolonged, recurrent within 24 hours), pretreatment with antibiotics that could mask meningitis, or age under 6 months. Observation of at least 1 to 4 hours allows clinical reassessment and parental education before discharge.
key_points: Simple febrile seizure: 6 months to 5 years, less than 15 min, generalised, single in 24 hours
LP not routine if fully immunised and well-appearing
LP for complex features, signs of meningitis, age under 6 months, or pretreatment with antibiotics
Antipyretics do not prevent febrile seizures
Recurrence risk ~30% lifetime
explanation.pearls: For first simple febrile seizure in a fully immunised infant over 6 months, the LP decision is driven by examination at hour 1, not by reflex on arrival - re-examine before deciding.

options.rationale: Lumbar puncture is no longer mandatory in a fully immunised infant over 6 months after a simple febrile seizure who is well-appearing; selective LP is the current approach. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizure; AAP)

Selective LP is recommended for first simple febrile seizure in a fully immunised infant over 6 months without signs of CNS infection; observe for clinical change and do LP only if features develop. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizure)
Empirical antibiotics for a presumed simple febrile seizure without features of bacterial infection are not indicated and may obscure later diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizure)
CT head is not indicated in a simple febrile seizure with normal neurology and conscious state; the seizure was brief, generalised and non-focal. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizure)

Immediate discharge after a first febrile seizure without an observation period and parental education risks early re-presentation and misses a window to identify atypical features. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizure)

explanation.summary: Paediatric status epilepticus algorithms in Australia use stepwise treatment: benzodiazepine (midazolam or lorazepam) at 5 minutes and 10 minutes, then non-benzodiazepine second-line agent at 15 to 20 minutes, then induction with intubation if refractory beyond 30 minutes. ConSEPT (Australia, NZ) and EcLiPSE (UK) trials showed levetiracetam and phenytoin have equivalent efficacy, with levetiracetam preferred for ease of administration, fewer cardiac side effects, and absence of QT prolongation risk. Loading dose 40 to 60 mg/kg over 5 minutes.
key_points: Two benzodiazepine doses maximum before second-line agent
Levetiracetam 40 to 60 mg/kg over 5 minutes - new first second-line in Australia
Phenytoin 20 mg/kg over 20 minutes alternative if levetiracetam fails
Refractory status (more than 30 min) needs anaesthetic induction and PICU
Avoid valproate in under-2s and in metabolic disease
explanation.pearls: Levetiracetam 40 to 60 mg/kg IV over 5 minutes is now the first second-line agent for paediatric status epilepticus - phenytoin only if levetiracetam is unavailable or has failed.

options.rationale: After two doses of benzodiazepine fail, IV levetiracetam 40 to 60 mg/kg is now first-line second-line therapy in Australian paediatric status epilepticus, with non-inferior efficacy to phenytoin and a better safety profile. (Source: RCH CPG: Status epilepticus; ConSEPT/EcLiPSE trials)

Phenytoin remains an acceptable second-line but levetiracetam is now preferred because of equivalent efficacy and fewer cardiac side effects; phenytoin is reserved when levetiracetam fails or is contraindicated. (Source: RCH CPG: Status epilepticus)

More than two benzodiazepine doses increase the risk of respiratory depression without improving seizure termination; move to a non-benzodiazepine second-line agent. (Source: RCH CPG: Status epilepticus)

Anaesthetic induction with intubation is reserved for refractory status (greater than 30 minutes despite two second-line agents) and requires PICU; it is not the immediate next step. (Source: RCH CPG: Status epilepticus)

Valproate is an alternative second-line but is avoided in children under 2 years and contraindicated in suspected metabolic disease; levetiracetam is the preferred first second-line in Australia. (Source: RCH CPG: Status epilepticus)

explanation.summary: Australian neonatal jaundice guidance uses age-in-hours bilirubin thresholds plotted on phototherapy and exchange transfusion nomograms, accounting for risk factors (prematurity, haemolysis, sepsis, low albumin). For a low-risk term infant the 60-hour phototherapy line sits around 320 micromol/L. Values close to but below the line trigger a 6 to 12 hour recheck. Always check for aetiology when bilirubin rises faster than 5 micromol/L per hour, total exceeds the 95th centile for age, or conjugated fraction is above 20 micromol/L (which always needs work-up).
key_points: Use age-in-hours nomogram - not absolute thresholds
Rising TSB by more than 5 micromol/L per hour warrants investigation
Conjugated bilirubin above 20 micromol/L always warrants work-up
Maintain breastfeeding alongside phototherapy
Exchange transfusion thresholds typically 80 to 100 micromol/L above phototherapy
explanation.pearls: Conjugated (direct) bilirubin above 20 micromol/L is never physiological and demands biliary atresia work-up; check stool colour and refer urgently if pale.

options.rationale: TSB is just below the phototherapy threshold; starting phototherapy without rechecking risks unnecessary mother-infant separation and feeding disruption. The trend matters more than the single value. (Source: RWH/RCH Neonatal jaundice guideline)
Discharge without rechecking TSB when the level is only 8 micromol/L below threshold risks crossing the threshold unobserved at home. (Source: RWH/RCH Neonatal jaundice guideline)

Exchange transfusion thresholds are typically 80 to 100 micromol/L above phototherapy and reserved for severe hyperbilirubinaemia; this TSB is well below. (Source: RWH/RCH Neonatal jaundice guideline)
Routine formula substitution is not recommended; breastfeeding support and re-evaluation is preferred even when phototherapy is indicated. (Source: RWH/RCH Neonatal jaundice guideline)

TSB is 8 micromol/L below the threshold for a low-risk term infant at 60 hours; the standard practice is to recheck in 6 to 12 hours and treat if the trajectory crosses the line. Investigate aetiology if rising. (Source: RWH/RCH Neonatal jaundice guideline)

explanation.summary: Iron overdose in children proceeds through five clinical stages: GI (first 6 hours), latent (6 to 24 hours), shock and metabolic acidosis (24 to 48 hours), hepatotoxicity (2 to 4 days), and late GI scarring (4 to 6 weeks). A 4-hour serum iron level above 90 micromol/L predicts systemic toxicity and is the threshold for IV desferrioxamine. Other indications include severe symptoms (haematemesis, altered mental status, persistent vomiting), metabolic acidosis, or unknown level with substantial ingestion. Treat for at least 24 hours; urine turns red-orange (vin rosé) as iron is excreted.
key_points: 4-hour serum iron above 90 micromol/L = chelation
Activated charcoal does NOT bind iron
Whole-bowel irrigation as adjunct for visible tablets on AXR
Desferrioxamine 15 mg/kg/hour IV, max 6 g/24 h
Stop chelation when urine clears and patient improves
explanation.pearls: A 4-hour serum iron above 90 micromol/L mandates IV desferrioxamine regardless of how well the child looks - the latent phase will end in shock if untreated.

options.rationale: Serum iron above 90 micromol/L with metabolic acidosis and systemic toxicity is an indication for IV desferrioxamine chelation; start at 15 mg/kg/hour and titrate. (Source: Poisons Information Centre - Iron; eTG Toxicology)
Activated charcoal does not bind iron and is not indicated in iron overdose; relying on it would miss the window for chelation. (Source: Poisons Information Centre - Iron; eTG Toxicology)
Lavage 4 hours post ingestion has poor yield and NAC is for paracetamol, not iron; this misses the chelation indication. (Source: Poisons Information Centre - Iron)
Whole-bowel irrigation may be an adjunct for radio-opaque tablets but does not replace chelation when systemic toxicity and high iron levels are present. (Source: Poisons Information Centre - Iron)
Bicarbonate does not address the iron toxin itself; acidosis is a marker of cellular injury and will improve with chelation, not isolated alkalinisation. (Source: Poisons Information Centre - Iron)

explanation.summary: ASCIA recommends a minimum 4-hour observation after IM adrenaline for anaphylaxis, extended for higher-risk patients including those requiring more than one adrenaline dose, severe presentations, asthmatics, history of biphasic reactions, ongoing allergen exposure, or limited access to emergency care. Biphasic reactions occur in approximately 5 percent of paediatric anaphylaxis cases, typically within 1 to 4 hours but up to 24 hours after initial resolution. Discharge planning includes a personalised ASCIA action plan, two adrenaline auto-injectors, allergy clinic referral, and clear safety-netting.
key_points: Standard observation 4 hours from last adrenaline dose
Higher-risk patients: more than one adrenaline dose, severe, asthma, biphasic history
Two EpiPens on discharge with ASCIA action plan
Allergy clinic referral for definitive testing
Steroids and antihistamines are adjunctive only
explanation.pearls: Any child who needed two IM adrenaline doses is in the higher-risk group - keep monitored for at least 4 hours from the second dose before discharge.

options.rationale: Oral steroids are not recommended routinely after anaphylaxis and do not justify shortening observation. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis guidelines)

Discharge soon after the second adrenaline dose does not allow biphasic reaction observation; ASCIA recommends a minimum 4-hour monitored period in this higher-risk group. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis guidelines)
Routine overnight admission is not required if the child remains well at 4 hours; clinical reassessment guides discharge. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis guidelines)
Steroids do not reduce biphasic reactions in the evidence base and are not a basis for early discharge. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis guidelines)

Patients who require more than one adrenaline dose are at higher risk of biphasic reactions and require a minimum 4-hour observation from the last adrenaline; ASCIA recommends this group are managed as higher risk. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis guidelines)

explanation.summary: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children, particularly in remote communities, have markedly higher rates of acute otitis media with perforation and chronic suppurative otitis media, with consequent hearing loss, language delay and learning impact. Australian remote-community guidelines (CARPA Standard Treatment Manual) recommend immediate high-dose amoxicillin (30 mg/kg BD) for 7 days for any acute otitis media episode in this population. Watchful waiting is reserved for non-Aboriginal children over 2 years with unilateral non-severe disease. Follow-up at 7 days is essential to assess resolution.
key_points: Aboriginal children with AOM: immediate amoxicillin, no watchful waiting
High-dose amoxicillin 30 mg/kg BD for 7 days
Follow-up at day 7 - if persistent perforation, treat as chronic suppurative otitis media
Topical ciprofloxacin drops added if discharge persists at 6 weeks (CSOM)
Screen siblings; coordinate ENT and audiology referral
explanation.pearls: In remote Aboriginal communities, an AOM perforation that persists past 6 weeks is chronic suppurative otitis media - escalate to topical ciprofloxacin ear toilet and ENT referral.

options.rationale: Watchful waiting is not appropriate for Aboriginal children, in whom otitis media has a higher risk of progression to chronic suppurative otitis media and hearing loss; immediate antibiotics are recommended. (Source: NACCHO/CARPA Standard Treatment Manual)

Aboriginal children with acute otitis media should receive immediate high-dose amoxicillin for 7 days because of the higher risk of perforation, persistent suppuration and hearing loss compared to non-Aboriginal children. (Source: NACCHO/CARPA Standard Treatment Manual; eTG: Antibiotic)

Topical ciprofloxacin is an adjunct in chronic suppurative otitis media but does not replace systemic antibiotics in acute otitis media with perforation in a high-risk child. (Source: NACCHO/CARPA Standard Treatment Manual)

Augmentin is reserved for treatment failure or recurrence within 4 weeks; high-dose amoxicillin remains the first-line agent in remote Aboriginal communities. (Source: NACCHO/CARPA Standard Treatment Manual)
Single-dose IM ceftriaxone is used when oral therapy is not feasible; here oral amoxicillin is appropriate and 7 days is needed for full course. (Source: NACCHO/CARPA Standard Treatment Manual)

explanation.summary: SUFE typically occurs in adolescents aged 10 to 16 years, more commonly male, obese or with endocrinopathy (hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency, hypogonadism). Knee or thigh pain is a classic referred pattern that delays diagnosis. The Klein line drawn along the superior femoral neck on AP view should intersect the femoral head epiphysis; failure to do so signals SUFE. Once diagnosed, the patient must not weight-bear, and urgent orthopaedic referral for in situ pinning is essential to prevent progression to chronic SUFE or avascular necrosis. The contralateral hip is at risk of subsequent SUFE in about 20 to 25 percent of cases.
key_points: Adolescent knee/thigh pain - examine the hip
Klein line failing to intersect epiphysis = SUFE
Strict non-weight-bearing from diagnosis
Urgent orthopaedic in situ pinning
Screen for endocrinopathy if atypical (under 10 yrs, very thin)
explanation.pearls: Any adolescent with knee or thigh pain and externally rotated leg gets an AP plus frog-leg lateral pelvis - and stays on the bed until orthopaedics reviews.

options.rationale: Outpatient management risks slip progression and femoral head avascular necrosis; SUFE is an urgent orthopaedic admission requiring strict non-weight-bearing and in situ fixation. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis)

SUFE is a surgical emergency once diagnosed; the patient must be made strict non-weight-bearing and referred urgently for in situ pinning to prevent progression and avascular necrosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis)
Plain radiographs are diagnostic; MRI delays definitive surgical management without changing immediate treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: SUFE)
Continued weight-bearing risks slip progression and AVN; SUFE patients must be non-weight-bearing from diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: SUFE)
He has no fever, no warmth, no inflammatory markers documented, and a Klein line consistent with SUFE; aspiration is not the next step. (Source: RCH CPG: SUFE)

explanation.summary: The Kocher criteria for differentiating septic arthritis from transient synovitis in a child with hip pain are: fever above 38.5 degrees C, non-weight-bearing on the affected side, ESR above 40 mm/hr, and WCC above 12 x10^9/L. Probability of septic arthritis rises from 3 percent at 0 criteria to over 93 percent at 4. CRP above 20 mg/L is a useful supplementary marker. Ultrasound demonstrates effusion; aspiration confirms diagnosis with cell count, Gram stain and culture. Treatment is urgent surgical washout plus IV antibiotics (flucloxacillin or cefazolin) targeting Staphylococcus aureus and Kingella kingae in younger children.
key_points: Kocher 4/4 = over 90% probability of septic arthritis
Ultrasound first imaging, aspiration confirms
Empirical IV flucloxacillin (or vancomycin if MRSA risk)
Surgical washout for confirmed septic arthritis
Differentiate from osteomyelitis with MRI if no effusion on US
explanation.pearls: Kingella kingae causes culture-negative septic arthritis in toddlers - ask the lab to inoculate joint fluid into a paediatric blood culture bottle for highest yield.

options.rationale: He meets 4 of 4 Kocher criteria (fever above 38.5, non-weight-bearing, ESR above 40, WCC above 12) which gives over 90 percent probability of septic arthritis; discharge is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Septic arthritis)
Empirical antibiotics without aspiration both impedes culture yield and risks discharge of an unrecognised septic joint that needs washout. (Source: RCH CPG: Septic arthritis)

With all 4 Kocher criteria positive, the post-test probability of septic arthritis is over 90 percent and definitive diagnosis requires ultrasound-guided aspiration; orthopaedic team must be involved urgently. (Source: RCH CPG: Septic arthritis; Kocher 1999)
MRI is useful when ultrasound is equivocal or osteomyelitis is suspected, but ultrasound is faster, cheaper and the first-line investigation here. (Source: RCH CPG: Septic arthritis)
Kocher criteria of 4/4 makes transient synovitis very unlikely; missing a septic joint risks joint destruction and sepsis. (Source: RCH CPG: Septic arthritis)

explanation.summary: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis presents at 3 to 8 weeks with progressive non-bilious projectile vomiting after feeds. Hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis arises from loss of HCl in vomit, aldosterone-driven potassium loss, and chloride-responsive renal bicarbonate retention. Pre-operative fluid correction is essential to reduce anaesthetic risk of apnoea and arrhythmia. Standard targets are chloride above 100 mmol/L, bicarbonate under 30 mmol/L, potassium above 3.5 mmol/L, and adequate urine output. Pyloromyotomy is then performed laparoscopically.
key_points: Pyloric stenosis: 3 to 8 weeks, non-bilious projectile vomiting
Hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis
Resuscitate with 0.9% saline; maintenance with K-containing fluid
Surgery only when Cl above 100, HCO3 under 30, K above 3.5
Pyloromyotomy is curative, feeding restored within 24 hours
explanation.pearls: In pyloric stenosis the operation can wait - the electrolytes cannot; aim chloride above 100 mmol/L and bicarbonate under 30 mmol/L before calling theatre.

options.rationale: Pyloric stenosis is a medical emergency until electrolytes are corrected, not a surgical emergency; anaesthesia in metabolic alkalosis risks post-operative apnoea and arrhythmia. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)

Pyloric stenosis is a medical-then-surgical problem; rehydration with 0.9 percent saline, then maintenance with potassium-containing fluid, correcting hypochloraemic hypokalaemic alkalosis until Cl over 100 and HCO3 under 30 before anaesthesia, is standard Australian practice. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)
Hartmann's contains lactate that is metabolised to bicarbonate and will worsen the alkalosis; 0.9 percent saline is preferred for resuscitation. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)
Pharmacological alkalosis correction is unnecessary and risks further electrolyte disturbance; volume and chloride replacement is the standard approach. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)
Pyloric stenosis is a mechanical obstruction; feeding via NG does not bypass the pyloric channel and delays definitive treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)

explanation.summary: Intussusception in children aged 3 months to 3 years is most commonly ileocolic and idiopathic, often after viral infection (lymphoid hyperplasia of Peyer's patches). Classic triad of intermittent abdominal pain, vomiting, and redcurrant jelly stool is present in fewer than 25 percent; ultrasound target sign is the diagnostic test of choice. Air enema reduction under fluoroscopy with surgical standby is the first-line treatment in a stable child without peritonism or perforation. Recurrence rate is 10 percent, mostly within 24 hours. Lead points (Meckel's, polyp, lymphoma) should be considered in children under 3 months or over 5 years, or after recurrence.
key_points: US target sign is diagnostic
Air enema first line - 80 to 90% success
Contraindications to enema: peritonism, perforation, shock
Recurrence 10%, most in 24 hours - keep monitored
Pathological lead point in atypical age or recurrence
explanation.pearls: Hartmann's, NG decompression and a surgical team standing by means safe air enema - the actual definitive reduction is by paediatric radiology.

options.rationale: Spontaneous reduction is rare and conservative management risks ischaemic complications; intussusception requires active reduction. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)
Surgery is reserved for failed enema, peritonism, perforation, or pathological lead point; air enema should be attempted first in stable children. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)
Air enema is preferred to barium because of lower perforation risk and avoidance of barium peritonitis; surgical standby is also mandatory. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

Air enema is the first-line management of ileocolic intussusception in a haemodynamically stable child without peritonism or perforation; it is successful in 80 to 90 percent and lower-radiation than barium. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)
Ultrasound is already diagnostic with the target sign; CT adds radiation without changing management. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

explanation.summary: Australian doctors are mandatory reporters of suspected child abuse in all states and territories. Concerning features include injuries inconsistent with history, multiple injuries at different stages, injuries in non-mobile infants (rolling at 4 to 6 months, sitting at 6 months), and delayed presentation. Workup includes skeletal survey (with repeat at 10 to 14 days), ophthalmology examination for retinal haemorrhages, abdominal imaging if bruising or markers, coagulation profile, neuroimaging if any signs, and full social work assessment. Admission ensures safety while child protection investigation occurs. Document objectively; do not confront parents about suspicion.
key_points: Injury in a non-mobile infant - presume NAI until excluded
Mandatory reporting to state child protection
Workup: skeletal survey, ophthalmology, coagulation, neuroimaging
Admission for safe assessment - do not discharge
Document factually; avoid confronting parents
explanation.pearls: Any injury in an infant under 6 months who is non-mobile (not rolling) demands a full NAI workup and admission - the differential of accidental trauma is vanishingly small.

options.rationale: Multiple unexplained injuries in an infant warrant mandatory child protection notification and full work-up; discharge would breach mandatory reporting obligations. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse; Australian state mandatory reporting)
Coagulation studies alone do not exclude non-accidental injury; multiple injuries with inconsistent history require full work-up and notification. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)
Notification is mandatory and is not contingent on parental agreement; delaying to negotiate risks the child's safety. (Source: Australian Mandatory Reporting)

Multiple unexplained injuries in a non-mobile infant trigger mandatory reporting; full work-up includes skeletal survey, ophthalmology for retinal haemorrhages, repeat coagulation studies, and admission for safe assessment. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse; Australian state mandatory reporting)
Outpatient referral does not meet the statutory threshold for mandatory reporting and risks ongoing harm; admission and notification are required now. (Source: Australian Mandatory Reporting)

explanation.summary: Hyperkalaemia management is staged: protect the myocardium (IV calcium gluconate), shift potassium intracellularly (insulin-dextrose, salbutamol, bicarbonate if acidotic), and remove potassium (resonium, dialysis). In children with CKD, dietary potassium loads from bananas, oranges and potatoes can precipitate dangerous hyperkalaemia. Pause ACE inhibitor or ARB. Calcium gluconate 10 percent 0.5 mL/kg IV over 5 minutes acts in 2 to 3 minutes and lasts 30 to 60 minutes; repeat if ECG changes persist after 5 to 10 minutes. Definitive management may require dialysis in CKD.
key_points: ECG changes = immediate IV calcium gluconate first
Insulin-dextrose, salbutamol, bicarbonate = intracellular shift
Resonium and dialysis = elimination
Pause ACE inhibitors/ARBs and review dietary load
Pseudohyperkalaemia in haemolysed sample - check repeat
explanation.pearls: Calcium gluconate 0.5 mL/kg of 10% (max 20 mL) is the only step that protects the myocardium within minutes - everything else only shifts or removes potassium.

options.rationale: Salbutamol lowers potassium by approximately 0.5 to 1.0 mmol/L but is slower than calcium gluconate; with ECG changes, membrane stabilisation is the first step. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperkalaemia)
Insulin-dextrose shifts potassium intracellularly but takes 15 to 30 minutes; ECG changes require immediate membrane stabilisation first. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperkalaemia)

Membrane-stabilising calcium gluconate is the immediate first step in hyperkalaemia with ECG changes; it acts within minutes to protect the myocardium while potassium-lowering treatments take effect. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperkalaemia)

Bicarbonate is reserved for acidotic hyperkalaemia and is less effective than calcium for membrane stabilisation; calcium gluconate should be first when ECG changes are present. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperkalaemia)
Resonium acts over hours and is not appropriate first-line when ECG changes demand minutes-fast action; it may be added later but is not the immediate intervention. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperkalaemia)

explanation.summary: Paediatric acute leukaemia (most commonly B-ALL at this age) presents with marrow failure (anaemia, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia), bone pain, lymphadenopathy and organomegaly. Tumour lysis syndrome (high urate, high potassium, high phosphate, low calcium) may precede or follow chemotherapy and is more common in bulky disease, high WCC, T-cell ALL and Burkitt lymphoma. Initial management is IV hyperhydration (2 to 3 times maintenance), allopurinol or rasburicase, monitoring electrolytes 4-hourly, and urgent transfer to paediatric oncology. Avoid potassium-containing fluids and minimise nephrotoxins.
key_points: Triad: marrow failure, bony pain, organomegaly
Tumour lysis: high K, urate, PO4, low Ca
IV hyperhydration without potassium
Allopurinol; rasburicase if urate above 0.5 mmol/L
Urgent paediatric oncology transfer
explanation.pearls: Rasburicase converts urate to allantoin and works within hours - reserve it for WCC above 100 x10^9/L or urate above 0.5 mmol/L; check G6PD first because it causes haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.

options.rationale: Pre-treatment steroids before tissue diagnosis can obscure leukaemia subtype and trigger tumour lysis without monitoring; treatment must be initiated by oncology after diagnosis. (Source: COG/ANZCHOG)
Outpatient management of suspected acute leukaemia with tumour lysis features is unsafe; he requires urgent admission and oncology referral. (Source: COG/ANZCHOG)

Newly suspected acute leukaemia with high WCC and biochemical tumour lysis features (high K, urate, phosphate, low calcium) requires urgent paediatric oncology transfer, IV hyperhydration and allopurinol or rasburicase. (Source: COG/ANZCHOG tumour lysis syndrome guidelines)
Bone marrow aspirate is essential but performed by the paediatric oncology team to ensure adequate sample, cytogenetics, and minimal residual disease testing. (Source: COG/ANZCHOG)
Routine imaging is not the next step; the priority is oncology transfer and tumour lysis prevention. Antibiotics are only added if febrile neutropenia is suspected. (Source: COG/ANZCHOG)

explanation.summary: Pertussis (whooping cough) in infants under 6 months carries the highest morbidity and mortality, particularly under 3 months who may present with apnoea, cyanosis and pulmonary hypertension rather than the classic whoop. Australian CDNA guidance is azithromycin 10 mg/kg once daily for 5 days as first-line treatment and post-exposure prophylaxis. Erythromycin is avoided in infants under 1 month because of pyloric stenosis association. Contact prophylaxis is offered to household members of any infant under 6 months, vulnerable adults (pregnant women in the third trimester, healthcare workers, childcare workers) and unimmunised under 1 year. Boostrix in third-trimester pregnancy is the most effective prevention.
key_points: Azithromycin first-line - 5 day course
Erythromycin avoided under 1 month (pyloric stenosis)
Post-exposure prophylaxis for household and at-risk contacts of infants under 6 months
Boostrix in 3rd trimester pregnancy is preventive
PCR + culture preferred over serology in acute illness
explanation.pearls: If a pregnant woman in the third trimester is in the household of a pertussis case and has not had a Boostrix booster in this pregnancy, she also needs azithromycin prophylaxis (and the booster as soon as practical).

options.rationale: Although antibiotics may not alter the cough course once paroxysmal, they reduce transmission and are recommended; contact prophylaxis is also needed. (Source: CDNA Pertussis SoNG)
Amoxicillin is not effective against Bordetella pertussis; macrolides are the first-line. (Source: CDNA Pertussis SoNG)
TMP-SMX is a second-line for macrolide intolerance and is not used in infants under 2 months; contact prophylaxis is also required. (Source: CDNA Pertussis SoNG)

Macrolide treatment of the index infant reduces transmission rather than altering clinical course this late, and post-exposure prophylaxis is offered to all household contacts of infants under 6 months. (Source: CDNA Pertussis SoNG; eTG: Antibiotic)
Erythromycin in infants under 1 month is associated with infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis; azithromycin is preferred in this age group. (Source: CDNA Pertussis SoNG)

explanation.summary: Late-onset neonatal sepsis (7 to 28 days) in a previously well term or late-preterm infant has a broad differential, including bacterial sepsis (E coli, group B Streptococcus, Listeria, late-onset coagulase-negative Staphylococcus), HSV (especially first-episode maternal genital HSV in late pregnancy), and meningitis. Empirical cover combines ampicillin + cefotaxime (or ceftriaxone if jaundice not severe) and aciclovir 20 mg/kg every 8 hours when there is any maternal HSV history, encephalopathy, seizures, vesicles, hepatitis, or thrombocytopenia. CSF, blood and surface swabs for HSV PCR should be obtained.
key_points: Late-onset sepsis differential: bacterial + HSV + Listeria
Empirical: ampicillin + cefotaxime + aciclovir
Aciclovir 20 mg/kg every 8 hours IV
First-episode maternal HSV near term = highest neonatal HSV risk
CSF, blood and surface HSV PCRs
explanation.pearls: A maternal first-episode genital HSV diagnosed after 34 weeks gestation gives the neonate a 30 to 50 percent vertical transmission risk; never empirically treat late-onset neonatal sepsis without IV aciclovir until HSV is excluded.

options.rationale: Empirical cover for an unwell late-preterm 9-day-old must include cefotaxime (or ceftriaxone if appropriate), ampicillin for Listeria and group B Streptococcus, and aciclovir for HSV given the maternal history. (Source: RWH/RCH Neonatal sepsis; ASHM Perinatal HSV)
Routine empirical antifungal cover is not indicated; Listeria cover and HSV cover are the priorities here. (Source: RWH/RCH Neonatal sepsis)
Flucloxacillin + gentamicin does not cover Listeria or HSV; this combination is more appropriate for late-onset Staphylococcus aureus sepsis. (Source: RWH/RCH Neonatal sepsis)
Vancomycin is not first-line in this scenario; ampicillin covers Listeria and group B Streptococcus more reliably, and HSV cover is missing. (Source: RWH/RCH Neonatal sepsis)

First-episode maternal genital HSV diagnosed late in pregnancy without antiviral suppression places the neonate at very high risk of HSV disease; ampicillin + cefotaxime covers bacterial sepsis and meningitis, and aciclovir 20 mg/kg every 8 hours covers HSV. (Source: RWH/RCH Neonatal sepsis; ASHM Perinatal HSV)

explanation.summary: This child has severe acute asthma refractory to first-line therapies (continuous bronchodilators and corticosteroids). The next appropriate step in the Australian step-wise management of paediatric status asthmaticus is an intravenous bolus of magnesium sulfate. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma Acute)
key_points: Severe asthma is characterised by agitation, inability to talk in sentences, severe work of breathing, and SpO2 < 92%.
Initial escalation involves bursts of inhaled bronchodilators transitioning to continuous nebulisers if no improvement.
When continuous nebulisers fail, the first-line intravenous adjunct is magnesium sulfate, followed by an IV salbutamol infusion if needed in an ICU setting.
explanation.pearls: A 'silent chest' or poor air entry indicates critically severe bronchospasm where wheeze may not be audible due to minimal airflow.

options.rationale: No anaphylaxis features (urticaria, angioedema, hypotension) despite peanut history; adrenaline is not indicated here. Would be correct only with confirmed anaphylaxis features (Source: ASCIA Acute Anaphylaxis).
Aminophylline is third-line in paediatric severe asthma, only after IV magnesium and IV salbutamol have failed. Would be correct as third-line in PICU (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma Acute).

Intubation in severe asthma is fraught with complications (bronchospasm, hypotension, barotrauma) and reserved for absolute respiratory arrest or exhaustion. Would be correct only with impending arrest after maximal medical therapy (Source: RCH CPG).

In a child with severe acute asthma failing continuous nebulised therapy and systemic corticosteroids, a bolus of intravenous magnesium sulfate is the next recommended step. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma Acute)
Asthmatic children may be mildly dehydrated, but fluid boluses do not relieve bronchospasm. Would be correct only for confirmed hypovolaemia, not primary asthma treatment (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Biliary atresia is the leading cause of paediatric liver transplantation in Australia, affecting about 1 in 15,000 livebirths. It presents with jaundice persisting beyond 2 weeks, pale (acholic) stools, dark urine, and a conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy restores bile drainage but its success is highly time-sensitive: operating before 60 days of age achieves jaundice clearance in around 70% of infants and significantly delays transplantation; after 90 days outcomes collapse. Any infant with prolonged jaundice (over 14 days term, 21 days preterm) must have fractionated bilirubin, LFTs, coagulation, urgent fasting hepatobiliary ultrasound, and prompt paediatric gastroenterology or hepatology referral. Differentials include neonatal hepatitis, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, choledochal cyst, and congenital infection (CMV, TORCH). Breast milk jaundice is a diagnosis of exclusion that requires unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and a thriving infant.
key_points: Any jaundice persisting beyond 14 days (or 21 days in preterm infants) requires fractionation of bilirubin.
Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is always pathological and never physiological or due to breast milk.
Biliary atresia presents with conjugated jaundice, pale (acholic) stools, dark urine, and hepatomegaly, requiring a Kasai procedure ideally before 60 days of life.
explanation.pearls: Any jaundice persisting beyond 14 days in a term infant (21 days in a preterm) needs a split bilirubin; conjugated fraction >20% of total or >25 micromol/L is cholestasis and biliary atresia must be excluded urgently because Kasai portoenterostomy outcomes fall sharply after 8 weeks of age (RCH CPG).

sources.label: RCH CPG: Jaundice in early infancy

options.rationale: Breast milk jaundice presents with unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia; this infant's conjugated fraction is severely elevated indicating cholestasis (biliary atresia until proven otherwise). (Source: RCH CPG: Jaundice).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Jaundice in early infancy

options.rationale: Phototherapy is only for unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia; in cholestasis it is ineffective and causes bronze baby syndrome. (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Jaundice in early infancy

options.rationale: Empirical treatment without ruling out time-critical surgical biliary atresia is inappropriate and delays definitive care. (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Jaundice in early infancy

options.rationale: HIDA scan is part of workup but US must be performed first to assess structural anatomy; timeline must be urgent, not routine outpatient. Would be correct only after urgent US (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Jaundice in early infancy

options.rationale: Pale stools, dark urine, and a conjugated bilirubin fraction >20% of total indicate pathological cholestasis. Biliary atresia must be urgently excluded via ultrasound as first-line imaging. (Source: RCH CPG: Jaundice in early infancy)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Jaundice in early infancy

explanation.summary: Paracetamol is the most common deliberate self-poisoning agent in Australian adolescents. Hepatotoxicity is from NAPQI, a reactive metabolite normally detoxified by glutathione; doses above 200 mg/kg or 10 g total deplete glutathione and produce fulminant liver failure within 72-96 hours if untreated. Acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione and is virtually 100% protective if started within 8 hours of a single ingestion. The Australian protocol is the 21-hour intravenous regimen (200 mg/kg over 4 hours, then 100 mg/kg over 16 hours), with extension based on paracetamol level, ALT and INR at end of infusion. The Rumack-Matthew nomogram applies only to single ingestions of immediate-release paracetamol with a known time and a level drawn 4-15 hours post-ingestion. For staggered ingestions, unknown time, sustained-release preparations, or any clinical concern, give acetylcysteine empirically without waiting for the level. Always involve NSW Poisons Information Centre (13 11 26).
key_points: The toxic threshold for acute paracetamol ingestion is 200 mg/kg or 10 g, whichever is less.
If the time of ingestion is unknown or staggered over more than 1 hour, start NAC immediately if the total dose ingested exceeds the toxic threshold.
The treatment nomogram is only valid for single acute ingestions presenting after 4 hours.
explanation.pearls: The Rumack-Matthew nomogram is invalid for staggered ingestions, unknown ingestion time, or sustained-release paracetamol; commence IV acetylcysteine empirically and run the 21-hour Australian regimen (200 mg/kg over 4h, then 100 mg/kg over 16h) (RCH CPG; NSW Poisons Information Centre).

options.rationale: In a potentially toxic paracetamol ingestion (>10g or 200mg/kg) where the time of ingestion is unknown or staggered, acetylcysteine must be started immediately without waiting for levels. (Source: RCH CPG: Paracetamol poisoning)

Activated charcoal is effective within 2 h of ingestion (4 h for sustained release); 7-h unknown window makes it unlikely beneficial. Would be correct within 1-2 h of ingestion (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Rumack-Matthew nomogram is strictly for single known-time acute ingestion; cannot be used in staggered or unknown timing. Would be correct only with single known-time ingestion (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Waiting for hepatotoxicity to manifest (24-72 h) misses the critical NAC window to prevent damage entirely. (Source: Australian PIC).
Bicarbonate is for TCA or severe salicylate overdoses; SSRIs and ibuprofen do not cause QRS widening. Would be correct only in TCA toxicity (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Non-accidental injury in infants is the second most common cause of paediatric trauma death in Australia, and the index injury that brings the child to attention is often relatively minor. Red flags include any fracture in a non-ambulant child, mechanism inconsistent with developmental stage or with examination findings, delay in seeking care, inconsistent histories, bruising in pre-mobile children (TEN-4 rule: torso, ear, neck in under 4-year-olds, or any bruise in an under-4-month-old), and pathognomonic injuries (classic metaphyseal lesions, posterior rib fractures, scapular fractures, retinal haemorrhage, subdural haematoma). Mandatory reporting applies to all medical practitioners in every state and territory - thresholds vary slightly but suspicion is sufficient. Management is admission to a safe environment, full skeletal survey, CT head and ophthalmology review where indicated, social work and child protection notification, and senior paediatric review. Never accuse caregivers - document objective findings only.
